en: Preface to the *Jìdēnglù* (Continuation of the Lamp Records): Throughout the successive generations of the Chan school, the transmission has been metaphorically likened to a lamp.

This is because it is capable of dispelling darkness to reveal all things, and also because it is capable of providing continuous illumination without end. It was during the Jingde era of the Song dynasty that Master Daoyuan first began compiling these records.
Following this, there appeared the *Guangdeng* (Extensive Lamp), *Xudeng* (Continued Lamp), *Lian deng* (Linked Lamp), and *Pudeng* (Universal Lamp).

Their accounts vary in detail and brevity, making it difficult for scholars to examine them all exhaustively. Consequently, Master Jì of Dàchuān compiled them into the *Huìyuán* (Source of the Assemblage).

This work provides a seamless continuity from beginning to end, greatly benefiting later students; his merit is indeed profound. As for the various masters from the Shàodìng era onwards, the *Huìyuán* had not yet...

As for those [works] that were collected, we still rely on the *Xùdēng* (Continued Lamp) to preserve them; yet even these are incomplete in their compilation, ceasing at the end of the Song and the beginning of the Yuan dynasties.

From the Yuan until the present day, nearly four hundred years have passed. The brilliance of many masters has been obscured and their luster extinguished, such that they have not yet attained clear renown in the world.
Who is to blame for this? Without deeming myself incompetent, I have extensively gathered materials this spring of the Wuzi year.

I searched extensively in the hope of compiling and supplementing previous omissions. In the summer of the Gengyin year, I further obtained the *Wǔdēng Xùlüè* (Abridged Continuation of the Five Lamps) compiled by Master Yuǎnmén Zhù, thereby supplementing what had not yet been prepared. Before long, however, my illness became extremely severe; it took three months for me to recover.
Upon recovery, my vision grew dim and my hearing grew dull, and my hands could no longer handle brush and inkstone. Therefore, his...
The records herein compiled still lack those from the Chenghua era onwards; this is because I have ceased at the point where it was necessary to cease.

The collection consists of six volumes and is titled *Jìdēng* (Continuing the Lamp). Some may argue that in the Chan school, the emphasis lies in mental awakening (*xīnwù*), and that language and written characters are but its dregs.
Why then must one compile volumes after volume and pages after page, entangling branches and extending vines as in the *Wǔdēng Hùyuán*? Moreover, [the present work] adds further...
Is this [work] merely a successor to the lamp? This would be to fail to realize that words can both obstruct the Way and carry the Way.
If one clings to them, even the refined essence becomes dregs; if one understands them, even the dregs become the refined essence. How could words then be entirely discarded?
As for the fact that what is recorded therein is sometimes detailed and sometimes brief, this is likewise due to the differences in time and the capacities of those to be taught.

The trend was such that it could not have been otherwise. For instance, the wall-gazing of the First Patriarch at Shaolin and the "settling the mind" of the Second Patriarch correspond to the administration by knotted cords of ancient times.
Subsequently, the *Xinxin Ming* and the *Dafabao Tanjing* correspond to the written characters of Emperor Xuan Yuan.
During the Tang dynasty, the two lineages of Mazu and Shitou expounded Chan in a vast and flourishing manner; this was not the ritual music of the Three Dynasties.
Indeed! In the Song dynasty, five schools vied with one another and five lamps emerged in succession. Are these not the Six Classics of Zhurong and Si?
When the times required brevity, even knotted cords were not considered too few; when the times required detail, even the Six Classics were not considered too many.

The essential point lies solely in adapting to the capacities of sentient beings to clarify their inherently existing nature. If one were to reprimand the people of the Spring and Autumn period, saying: "Why do you not..."
To bind together slips of wood with knotted cords—is this not contrary to reason? That such works continue to be produced to this day is not because it can be helped;

it is simply like how, after the Six Classics, there appeared the Seven Chapters of Mencius, which clarify the Way of the former kings by asserting that human nature is good, extolling Yao and Shun, promoting benevolence and righteousness, and silencing heterodox doctrines. How could one say that these were added [to the Classics] to increase them?

How lamentable! If that which has been recorded is confused and impure, failing to accord with the intent of the West’s arrival [the Buddha's teaching], then it would be like Wang Tong’s Five Classics;
though he claimed they could succeed those of Confucius, he was unaware that they were in fact a farce of "dust for rice and mud for soup.
Is the gravity of such a transgression not indeed great? This is what I deeply fear and cannot escape.
I shall still submit this to the Great Square (the masters of the Dharma) to await their chiseling and refinement.
Written on an auspicious day during the latter part of the ninth month of the year of Xinmao, by the monk Yuanxian, a successor to the Patriarchs of Gushan,
in the Shengjian Hall.
General Principles:
There were originally five schools; now there are only two, the Linji and Caodong.

Since the *Huìyuán* (Anthology of Sources) for the Linji school concludes with the seventeenth generation, this record begins with the eighteenth generation. The *Huìyuán* for the Caodong school concludes... [text ends]
Since the records for the fifteen preceding generations have been lost, this compilation begins with the sixteenth generation.
Any dharma-discourse of the various masters that has not survived but whose provenance can be verified shall be recorded;

likewise, those who possessed even a single praiseworthy deed or exhibited some extraordinary circumstance at the time of their death shall also be recorded. This is so that people may not regard the lineage of our school as merely a succession of empty names.
This is also like beating a drum with the mouth.
Among the various masters, there are some whose names are known but whose sources and recorded sayings have been lost;

these are retained according to established precedent so that future generations may examine them and include them. Those who have verses on ancient cases (*songgu*) that have been transmitted to the world are likewise selected.
One or two [passages] have been appended herein; this follows the precedent of the *Xùlèi*. We shall follow this now as well.

As for the words and phrases of various masters, some may contain a mixture of the refined and the flawed; it is difficult to record them all indiscriminately, yet how could they be entirely discarded?
I have now selected and excerpted from it for two reasons: first, to complete the excellence of my predecessors; second, because even fragments of gold or shards of jade are nothing but treasures.
The single volume *Wudeng xulu* (Continued Brief Record of the Five Lamps) is particularly detailed in its collection and transcription; much that I had not previously seen was obtained from it.
This book is of great merit. However, there are matters that I have seen which he has not yet seen; there are passages that he has included while I have omitted;
there are cases where the same discourse record (*yulu*) is treated differently in terms of inclusion or exclusion;
and there are instances where the same biographical account (*xingshi*) varies in its detail or brevity. For these reasons, I have compiled this record here.
This cannot be avoided. How could one venture to act against its merit?
Regarding the sequence of the Five Houses, both the *Jingde Chuandeng Lu* and the *Zhengzong Ji* place Qingyuan before Nanyue.
Daishū was a partisan of his own school who placed Nan-yueh first and Qingyuan second;

furthermore, fearing that others might dispute this, he again placed Hogen before Linji. This was an extreme state of confusion. Now, we shall establish the order according to the established precedent.

Since the dates of the various masters are remote, it is difficult to verify their lineages with certainty. I have heard that during the early Ming dynasty there was a *Xu chu deng lu* (Continued Record of the Transmission of the Lamp), but I have not had the opportunity to see it, and it has long since ceased to be transmitted.
Only during the Jiajing era was there a *Zu pai tu* (Chart of Patriarchal Lineages) which recorded them in considerable detail;

however, it is extremely chaotic and cannot be relied upon entirely. Recently, I have seen the *Wudeng xulu* (Continued Brief History of the Five Lamps), which provides a truly excellent verification and rectification.
It is extensive, yet still not exhaustive. For instance, there is the "Moon Forest Mirror" (Yuelin Jing) beneath Dongyu Island in the sea.

Upon examination, it appears that Yuelin was one who entered the Way as a person of original nature; he was actually the eighty-first abbot of Jingshan and passed away in the Year of Yimao during the Zhengde era.
Since he lived at a great distance from Dongyu, he has been specifically excluded. Other matters have not yet been rectified.
I leave this matter for future gentlemen to judge.

Chan Master Changweng Ru Jing of Tiantong Monastery in Mingzhou was a dharma successor of Chan Master Xuedou Jian. From birth, he was exceptionally gifted; he did not behave like a common child. As he grew up, he studied the world-transcending Dharma.
He went to Xuedou to study under Zu’an, where he attained realization while contemplating the kōan of the "Cypress Tree in the Courtyard. He presented this verse:
He said: "The meaning of the Ancestors from the West is the cypress tree in front of the courtyard; nostrils vast and empty, facing the eyes.

As soon as the withered branch that has fallen to the ground leaps up, the pine and ivy laugh aloud in exuberance. Yan'an approved of this. He subsequently moved through various famous monasteries in his public career, later presiding over Jingci and ascending to Tiantong.
On the occasion of opening the furnace, he ascended the hall, called the assembly together, drew a circle, and said: "This is Tiantong."
The brazier: approach it and you are burned to death; retreat and you are frozen to death. Suddenly, a man comes forth and asks, "What should be done?
[The Master] says: "The brazier has moved! Ascending the hall, he said: "The frosty wind howls with a chilling severity; frosty leaves fall in a desolate rustle."
Raising his whisk, he said: "Look! Only this Linglong Peak rises ever higher. This so-called 'heavenly child’s滞货 (stale goods)' is being sold today at a short market price.
Is there anyone here who can offer a price? He descended from the seat and went on a tour of the hall. Ascending the hall again, he said:
"Not letting anything enter from without, not letting anything go out from within—strike one decisive blow and all matters are finished. But tell me, how is it? Taibai.
Before the peak, he brings forth something entirely new; both internal and external regulations are fully entrusted to him. He ascends the hall and says:
"Tiantong’s iron-stink old fist strikes down the water-buffalo of the rivers and lakes. At nightfall, suddenly an egg is born;
at daybreak, it pushes out the great sun. Tell me, what does this mean? It is to dry the dampness of everyone present, so that your steps shall not slip as if on oil."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Where Lingyun saw it, the peach blossoms were in bloom; where Tiantong sees it, the peach blossoms have fallen.
The peach blossoms bloom—driven by the spring breeze. The peach blossoms fall—the spring breeze is harsh. Setting aside Lingyun for a moment, is there anyone who meets Tiantong?

When the spring breeze is harsh, the peach blossoms leap over the waves, their heads and horns emerging. [He] then pushed [the seat] to ascend the hall for the newly established Miaoyan Repentance Ceremony.
Upside-down, many rat nests have grown; swept clean across the level ground, he laughs heartily. From emptiness he erects a towering structure;
he covers over donkeys and oxen, never weary of the multitude. Today, the great conditions are fulfilled for all eternity, bringing forth this Great Matter.
But tell me, how so? "He rubs his forehead, leaving it to the guests outside the gate; once home, he returns it to those within. Again, he cites the passage from Wén:
Wenshu asked, "Where has Mañjuśrī recently been? Mañjuśrī replied, "To the South. Wenshu asked, "How is the Dharma maintained in the South?
Mañjuśrī said, "In this age of the final dharma (*mofa*), the bhikṣus there rarely observe the precepts.

Wenshu asked, "How large is their assembly? Mañjuśrī said, "Either three hundred or five hundred. The Master [Dongshan] said, "The spring breeze entices the partridge to cry. Mañjuśrī then asked, "Wenshu, this..."

[The Master] asked, "How do you maintain the Buddha-dharma? Xuanzhushan said, "Ordinary people and sages dwell together; dragons and snakes are intermingled. [The Master] asked, "How many followers do you have?
Xuanzhushan said, "Three times three before, and three times three after. The Master said, "Waves and ripples on level ground; an iron ship with a hook."
These two turns of phrase must be used to pluck the eyebrows of those from all quarters.

Furthermore, there are two more turns of phrase to be used to open the eyes of those from all quarters—perhaps three hundred, perhaps five hundred—copper coins or iron coins, the count complete and the value full. "The three threes before and the three threes after.
Radishes and taro tubers, shallowly stored yet filling the entire load. Suddenly, the eyes of those from all quarters will be opened; it is certain.
[The Master] clapped his hands and laughed loudly. "What are you laughing at? If you do not laugh at the 'Bacha' [the rustic], then you must laugh at the 'fabricated' (duzuan).

all are together within the painted scroll. Regarding the Master’s six times sitting in the seat of enlightenment, he did not speak of his lineage transmission. The assembly...
This was his request. The Master said, "I shall bring it forth in the Nirvana Hall. Indeed, at the time of his death, he offered incense and said:

The Japanese Zen Master Dōgen of Eiheiji was surnamed Minamoto. He was a ninth-generation descendant of Emperor Shōmu. His physical features were extraordinary and elegant;
his seven parts of the body were full and even, and his eyes possessed the double pupils of a sage. At the age of seven, he studied the *Mao Shi* and the *Zuo Zhuan*.
Furthermore, he naturally mastered various sutras and histories without relying on a teacher’s instruction; at that time, he was acclaimed as a "Divine Child.
While observing his mother’s mourning, he watched as incense smoke curled upward and vanished moment by moment, through which he realized the impermanence of the world.

He subsequently entered the monastic life under Dharma Master Liangxian of Mount Tai, following his maternal uncle, at the age of fourteen. He soon received full ordination and exhaustively studied both the Mahayana and Hinayana teachings.
Relying upon various sutras and treatises, he heard that in Great Song there were veteran masters who transmitted the Buddha’s mind-seal.
He therefore specially boarded a ship and crossed the sea to enter Song, arriving at Mingzhou during the sixteenth year of the Jiading era of Emperor Ningzong.
He first ascended Mount Tiantong to see the monk Wujie Pai; subsequently, he traveled to Shuangjing to pay respects to Zeweng Yan, and further visited Zongyue and Yuetang.
Among the many eminent elders who were present, there was none whose spiritual resonance did not harmonize with his own.
As they were about to depart, the venerable Jiyu exhorted him, saying, "Among those in the present day who possess the great eye of the school, none is like Master Jing, Changweng.

He is currently residing at Tiantong by imperial decree; you should go to see him. Following these instructions, the Master went to Tiantong. Upon meeting him, he felt as joyful as if they had been old acquaintances. The Master—
Dōgen then addressed him, saying: "Since my youth, I have cultivated the bodhicitta in my own country and studied under various masters.

Yet, though I perused the sutras and śāstras, I remained mired in mere names and concepts and failed to comprehend the Great Dharma. Later, upon entering the Great Song, I met with several venerable elders and was fortunate enough to hear the Linji tradition.
Now that I am able to attend this Dharma assembly, it is truly a blessing for many lifetimes. I pray that the Venerable Master will compassionately grant me your ear."
Dōgen frequently entered the inner quarters to inquire about the essentials of the Dharma; for the matter of birth and death is great, and time does not wait for man.
Ryūkan, moved by his sincerity, joyfully granted him permission. Thereupon, the Master practiced with such diligent effort day and night that his side did not touch the mat for nearly two years.

[The Master] said, "My mind has fallen away. How can you simply keep on sleeping? The Teacher heard this from the side; at that moment, his body and mind fell away, and he attained a vast, clear realization.

"At a crossroads," [Zhaozhou] said. "Master, do not mistakenly stamp me. Jing said, "I do not mistakenly stamp you.

Recognizing that the eyes are askew and the nose is straight, one is no longer deceived by others; thus, one returns home empty-handed, possessing not even a hair’s breadth of Buddha-dharma.
It is simply a matter of passing the time as it unfolds: day after day the sun rises in the east, night after night the moon sinks in the west.

Listen to the words beyond the cry of the partridge. Ascending the hall: It has been a long time since Xingsheng has spoken for the assembly.
The Buddha Hall, the Sangha Hall, the sound of the stream, and the shadows of the trees have all already explained it for you. Have you heard it yet? If you say...
"I have heard of it. "What did he say? "If you say you did not hear it, you will betray yourself.
Lord Yizhong, the Governor of Yunzhou, established the Yongping Monastery and invited the Master to reside there.

On the day of the opening of the hall, a mountain deity appeared, and for this reason the mountain was named Mount Jixiang (Auspiciousness). At that time, Master Lai Ping received the Bodhisattva Great Precepts from the Master.
He observed the etiquette of a disciple with great reverence. His disciples, both ordained and lay, who had received the precepts, were spread throughout the Eastern Land.
Later, Emperor Saga conferred upon him the robe of high rank and a posthumous title; the Master placed these on a high shelf and never wore them upon his body.

One day, manifesting a slight illness, he took leave of the assembly, wrote a verse, and passed away while sitting upright. Upon cremation, countless *śarīra* relics were obtained, and they were enshrined in a stupa at Eikō-ji. [End of excerpt]
He lived for fifty-four years and spent forty-one summer retreats in seclusion.

His writings include the *Zhengfayan zang* (The Treasury of the True Dharma Eye), the *Conglin qinggui* (Pure Rules for the Forest of Monasteries), the *Xuedao yongxin ji* (Collection on the Application of Mind in Studying the Way), and various recorded sayings (*yulu*) totaling several volumes, all of which have circulated in the world.
During the Jingding era, the monk Wuwai Yuan once composed a preface to his recorded sayings. [His disciples included] Ning of Lingyin Tui-geng and Xutang of Jingci.
Both I, Yu, and Lao have provided colophons for this work. His Dharma-heir disciples are three: Huicong, Senghaiquan, and Huifan.

The sword for executing the sycophants within the cubit-long casket; the letter of recommendation for the worthy within the hundred pouches and boxes. The Guest within the Host says: "The whips are stilled at the vermilion steps as the six palaces open;

If a cart does not move, one must strike the ox. Now, you have struck the ox; has the cart moved yet? The Master said: "The pure breeze you unload—whom do you entrust it to?"
Chan Master Xuedou Wuyin Dazheng of Mingzhou was a dharma heir of Chan Master Tiantong Xiuzhi. He was the son of the Shi family of Poyang in Raozhou. From his youth, he was exceptionally intelligent;

he relied upon Changguo Temple in that prefecture to receive the tonsure and full ordination. Later, he traveled abroad to pay his respects to Jingshi Yan at Yuan Tong, where his spiritual faculties were awakened.

Their words did not accord. At that time, Sian Rui was residing in a secluded room; the Master attended him daily for rigorous training. Hearing that Yunwai was teaching the Way at Tiantong, the Master went to rely upon him.
One day, during a private interview, their spiritual dialogue reached a point of accord, and he subsequently received his transmission (the dialogue is found in the chapter on Yunwai).
In the ninth year of the Zhizheng era, he presided over Xuedou. He ascended the hall and said: "A thousand explanations and ten thousand expositions are not equal to a single face-to-face encounter."
Yesterday was the twenty-ninth; this morning is the first day of the seventh month. I inform you, seekers of the profound mystery: time passes as swiftly as a flying arrow.
Those two eyes born of your mother, each as black as lacquer—hurry, hurry, turn your heads back and behold the Buddha of True Nature!
After a long silence, he said, "What kind of face is this? He descended from his seat and went around the hall to drink tea.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Is it marvelous? Most patch-robed monks have no nostrils at all. Is it profound? At the top of the banner pole, there is no blue sky.

A man of resolve cannot bear to fold his hands; how could a fine horse wait for the whip? Completely transcending the staff and shout, they do not fall into the trap of words. When spring comes, the hundred birds do not fail to arrive."
He passed away once more. Having found respite in his mountain retreat, he was able to sleep until high noon. After residing there for four years, he retired to the Yuanming Hermitage at Dingshui.
The following year, he manifested parinirvāṇa; his body was cremated and a stupa was erected behind the hermitage.
The Chan Master Wángshān Tǐ of Tàiyuán Prefecture, a twenty-generation successor under Chan Master Dàmíng Bǎo of the Qīngyuán lineage,
served Dàmíng for ten years with diligent effort, personally acting as his attendant. [He kept this] secret.
Because he was so profoundly dignified and grave, no one came to study under him. One day, when he packed his bedding to leave, everyone was filled with suspicion and wonder.

Someone asked the attendant of Daming, "Where is he going? Daming replied, "He comes from all quarters and goes to all quarters; why take it to heart? Another asked, "What is it like to study the Way?
Daming said, "If the Way exists, studying it grows one's character; if the Way does not exist, studying it diminishes one's majestic radiance. The assembly [was thus enlightened].
Only then did he realize that he had already received the seal of approval. He remained hidden for a long time in the Western Mountains at Taiyuan Prefecture.
The prefectural administration and both government offices invited him to reside at Wangshan to establish a Zen monastery. The Master once elucidated the principles of the Dongshan school, saying:

"Since there is a position of supreme dignity, one must clarify the person of supreme dignity; yet one must know that the person of supreme dignity does not occupy the position of supreme dignity—only then is it truly understood."
The Honored One is noble and does not fall into hierarchical stages. The verse on the five positions says: Centered within the Deviation: Deep night in the ancient hall, light smoke locks the doors;
Silent and still, moss seals the ground where subjects do not stand; Dense and profound, the radiance lies before any sign appears. Deviation centered within the Center:

The jade artisan does not behold his own face in the mirror upon the dais; At the hour of midnight, the stars and river-mist are thick; As ever, the green mountain does not reveal its peak. Centered within the Center...
Come! A wooden man, carrying his staff, turns back from within the flames; he rouses the clay ox to plow the refined colors, letting the stone horse stride upon the green moss.
Reaching the "partial" (pian): turning and meeting, they fully manifest their spirit; though they brandish weapons together, they never clash at the sharp edge.
In this great function,纵横 (zōnghéng), there is no change or variation. Reaching the "combined" (jiān): when light and dark are exhausted, even time does not shine; the stone woman possesses wisdom.
Its subtlety is difficult to fathom. It is the understanding that plants grow upon the summit where roots are severed.
Among the five ranks, the fourth rank has traditionally been known as "Arriving from Within Both" (jiānzhōng zhì).

Later, Hong Juefan failed to grasp this principle and erroneously changed it to "Arriving from Within Partiality" (piānzhōng zhì). However, in reality, no one under the Dongshan lineage has ever followed this [alteration]. It is like the sky...
Tongjue, Jingci Hui, and others all utilized the "reaching through the middle" (jiānzhōng zhì); this can be seen in the *Huìyuán* and various other texts.
By the end of the Song dynasty, Master Tian Tongjing did not speak of his lineage at all during his lifetime;

it was only at the time of his death that he offered incense to signify his succession of Xuedou. Examining his preaching, although he possessed a gate of awakening, he merely expounded according to his own inclination.

The fundamental intent has been entirely lost. Thus, when Lukmen succeeded Tiantong in composing the *Wuwei Song* (Verses on the Five Ranks), he first employed the sequence "partial → middle → ultimate.
Subsequently, this was transmitted through five generations, each with their own verses; yet, only those composed by Wangshan are appropriate.
Nevertheless, they still employ the sequence "partial → middle → ultimate," which is an adherence to Lukmen’s error and a failure to recognize it as such.
Chan Master Renshan Heng attended Da Ming for a long time and eventually ascended to the innermost sanctum. Ming bestowed upon him the robe and the Dharma.
The Master said, "I am not such a person. Ming replied, "If you are not such a person, it will not bring harm to you.
Out of deep affection for the milk of the Dharma, the Master bowed his head and accepted. Ming instructed him, saying, "Since you are thus, first of all, you must not..."
It is easy to transcend the world. However, if one is impetuous and frivolous, there will inevitably be setbacks along the way.
This is the lineage of Chan Master Wushan Ti, the twenty-first generation descendant of Qingyuan.
When Chan Master Xueyan Man of Daming in Cizhou first visited Puzhao, Puzhao said, "Brother, you are young and vigorous;
this is precisely the time to exert yourself in inquiry and study. In my own youth, every thought was constantly devoted to the Buddha-dharma.
The Master left his seat and stepped forward, asking, "How about now, Preceptor? Puzhao replied, "It is like being with an enemy. The Master said, "If..."
"If I had not received these words, I would have traveled nearly a thousand li for nothing. He then descended from his meditation seat, took the Master’s hand, and said, "A true master, indeed!
The Master had once practiced with Shengmo, and on one occasion had knelt before him while receiving his scolding.

When someone asked him the reason for this, the Master replied, "Nowadays in various quarters, there are teachers and their disciples or dharma-kin who engage in disputes and litigation, inviting public ridicule. This is like a worm within the body of a lion devouring its own flesh."

One must not fail to issue this solemn admonition. Later, Cān resided at Mount Wangshan and clarified the Mind-Seal (Citta-mudrā). He succeeded [his predecessor] as abbot. Upon ascending the hall for formal discourse, he cited Dongshan, saying:
"At the end of autumn and the beginning of summer, brothers, whether you go east or west, you must head toward a place ten thousand *li* away where there is not a single blade of grass.
After a long silence, he said: "But what about that place ten thousand *li* away where there is not a single blade of grass? How is it?"
[The Master] said, "Go! Shishuang said, "As soon as you step out the door, it is all weeds. Dayang said, "Even if you do not step out the door, it is still a vast expanse of weeds.
The Master said, "Although these three old fellows speak with one voice, they cannot avoid bumping heads and knocking foreheads.
Why? One has opened his mouth wide and cannot close it; another has raised his foot high and cannot lower it."
Below. One person, having tightly closed the door, cannot go out. King Shan was not like this: the entire realm of the ten directions is not outside;
it is entirely within a single mote of dust. That single mote of dust is not inside; it is entirely pervasive throughout the realm of the ten directions.
Even this mere measure of a single mote of dust must be exhausted to the point of non-attainability. Where could one set up a door there? Where could one enter the grass? Do you understand?
Do not encroach upon the autumn grasses of Dongling; please look instead at the lotus of Shushan in mid-winter.
Chan Master Shengmo Guang once composed a verse on Jiufeng’s refusal to accept the Head Seat, saying: "The Head Seat needlessly lost a single stick of incense;
Jiufeng was not suppressing a man of high talent. If one were to take 'one color' as the true succession, one would betray the former master."
On the occasion of borrowing [a robe], he addressed the assembly. He cited the story of Magu shaking his staff and said: "Right is not right; wrong is not truly wrong. Right and wrong have no master;
the myriad virtues all return to the same source. The owl and the cock, day and night, merely waste their efforts in fragmentation.
I, who lack the three inches [of tongue], can call a turtle a tortoise; Kāśyapa was unwilling, so let him frown as he pleases."
Chan Master Wansong Xingxiu of Ba’en Temple in Yanjing was a native of Henei.
He was of the Cai clan. He descended from the twenty-second generation below Qingyuan and was a dharma heir of Chan Master Xueyan Quan. He emerged from...
He was born into a family in Jingtu Monastery in Xingzhou and took the master Yūn as his teacher. Later, he received full ordination.

Carrying his satchel, he traveled from Yan, passing through Tan and visiting Qingshòu Monastery to attend upon the elder Shèngmò. The master instructed him to contemplate the saying, "Turning the self back into mountains, rivers, and the great earth," spoken by Changsha.
For half a year, he made no progress at all. Shèngmò said, "I only wish that you would realize it late. One day, there was...

He reflected further on the saying that Xuansha had not yet reached the ultimate. Seeking instruction from Xueyan at Daming in Zhi, within twenty-seven days he suddenly realized his own artifice was exhausted.
Xueyan kept him in the administrative office; their words were in perfect accord, and he was immediately entrusted with the robe and verse.

He subsequently returned to Jingtu, where he built the Wansong Pavilion for his own enjoyment. Later, the venerable elders of the monastery earnestly requested him to serve as abbot, and he resided there in succession.
Small Assembly at Wanshou Monastery in Zhongdu. In the past, there was a man riding a donkey who asked the assembly of monks, "Where is the Way-place?
A monk replied, "It is toward the Way-place. The man said, "Where is it that this is not the Way-place? The monk struck him with his fist and said, "This fellow has no sense of propriety!
He rides a donkey across the Way-place and does not dismount. The man was left speechless. The Master said, "Everyone says this..."
The Han has a head but no tail; yet you fail to realize that this monk’s earlier words do not accord with his later ones.

Since you already know that every lifting and placing of the foot is a site of enlightenment (*dōjō*), why do you not awaken to the fact that riding on a donkey or a horse is nothing other than a Buddha-activity?

In the fourth year of the Mingchang era of Emperor Jin Zhangzong (which was the fourth year of the Shaoxi era of Emperor Guangzong of the Southern Song), the Emperor issued an edict for the Master to ascend the seat within the imperial palace.

The Emperor personally received him with ceremonial rites and heard the Dharma never before heard, attaining awakening and profound reflection. He personally presented the Master with a magnificent *saṃghāṭī* robe of brocade and silk.

The ladies of the inner court and the nobility prostrated themselves and knelt in reverence, each offering their most cherished treasures. In the second year of the Cheng’an era, the year Ding-si, the Emperor again issued an edict.
The Master resided at Xiying Chan Temple on Mount Yang in the capital. Ascending the hall, he spoke this verse: "The Lotus Palace is specially constructed as a Brahma Hall;
To traverse the sacred realm, one must be a sage on horseback. After the rain, the waters are clear and birds float upon them;
As the rosy clouds brighten, the mountains are still, draped in brocade. Even Tang Cheng could unfurl the vast celestial net, And Lü Wang rarely lowered his moon-dipping hook. I ask you now:

The scenery is truly a magnificent season; it is autumn in a world of gold, with the osmanthus trees in bloom. The Master asked a monk, "Dongshan said, 'The dragon roars in the withered tree—its extraordinary resonance is difficult to hear.
What is this extraordinary resonance? The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "You have a fine understanding of the dragon's roar."
Question: "The Buddhas do not appear in the world; why then are they born in royal palaces? The Master said: "The blue sky constantly lifts its feet. Question: "There is also no nirvana;
why then do they pass away beneath the twin śāla trees? The Master said: "The bright sun does not shift its wheel. Question:
"As for those who have let go on that other side, why do they not abide in the position of correctness? The Master said: "Great merit."

[The Master] said, "Not acting as a master. [A monk] asked, "Why does the person who turns their head toward this side not fall into a heterodox path? The Master said, "Ultimate transformation is non-action.

[The Master] asked, "I told you before: do not go; returning is to turn one's back on one's father. How can one avoid turning one's back on one's father? The Master said, "Above all, do not turn your head.
[The Master] asked, "It is difficult to let go of mind after mind. What is the person who lets go? The Master said, "Carrying."
[The Master] took it away. He asked: "In this place, there is no Maitreya and no Sudhana; why then do you say that on the crystal palace there is no teacher?
The Master said: "When the palace has been demolished, come and see me. He moved to reside at Baoyuan (Baoen). Later, he retired to Congrong An and addressed the assembly:
"Where the wheel of the Dharma turns, even the eye of wisdom remains deluded; when the precious mirror is opened, not a speck of dust can pass."
The raised fist does not touch the ground; responding to things, one must know the proper time. When two blades meet, how can one avoid them?
To the assembly: if you leave, I will detain you; if you stay, I will send you away. Neither leaving nor staying—He has no land; where could one meet Him?
Everywhere, at every place—tell me, what kind of thing is so extraordinary? To the assembly: if it moves...
"Burying oneself ten thousand fathoms deep—if one does not move, sprouts will grow right where one stands. You must loosen both ends and let go of the middle;
only then can you buy straw sandals and travel the path. To the assembly: Kicking over the vast ocean, the great earth flies into dust;
shouting away the white clouds, empty space shatters to pieces. Even the strict raising of the true command is but half-raised. When the Great Function is fully manifested—"
How is it established? To show the assembly: "The single pivot of the upward path is like a crane soaring into the Milky Way;
the direct route facing the sun is like a hawk flying over Silla. Even if one’s eyes were like shooting stars, one could not avoid having a mouth like a flat carrying pole.

Tell me, what is the essential principle here? He once clarified the essential principle of the Dongshan school, saying: "Muzhou said, 'To tear it open is up to me; to fold it back together is also up to me.'"
If you ask about "tearing asunder," he immediately lifts up a bundle of rope; if you ask about "gathering together," he immediately clasps his hands and sits.

Although he is thus able to withdraw and extend at will, it is very much like being put to work by another. Dongshan condemned this as splitting a single statement into two parts—like a missing needle and a broken thread.
Have you not heard it said: "To speak in such a way is easy; to maintain continuity is also very difficult"? You must simply remain present and correct.
Vanishing. It is rolled up yet ever more expansive; its interlocking hooks and rings are called the "unbroken bloodline.
It is also said that the single school of Yaoshan is truly difficult to succeed. When Yunyan sweeps the floor, the dust rises to the heavens;

Luopu takes this to heart and voices his grievance without end. It is well that the tongueless man can speak and the handless man can strike. Even if the staff and the shout were to fly back and forth, [it would still be so].

He could only grasp half of it by holding it alongside [the other texts]. The Master was extensively versed in all the various schools of learning, including those of the Duke of Zhou, Confucius, Laozi, Zhuangzi, and the hundred other traditions.

He read through the Tripitaka three times and constantly took the Avataṃsaka Sūtra as his primary practice. One hundred and twenty people attained the Dharma from him. He lived to the age of eighty-one.
The stupa is located north of Qianxi Bridge within the city of Yanjing.
It is the memorial of Chan Master Ba’en Xiū, the twenty-third generation descendant under Qingyuan and the dharma heir of [his predecessor].
Chan Master Fuyü of Shaoshi Xueting in the Western Capital was the son of the Zhang family of Wenshui in Taiyuan.

When the Master reached the age of five, he understood speech and could master a thousand words a day; thus, his village gave him the nickname "The Holy Child. Not long after, he encountered the hardships of the world's turmoil.

Having lost his kin, he was solitary and without support. On the road, he encountered an elderly bhikṣu who urged him to leave the household life and study the Buddha’s teachings, saying, "If you can recite one fascicle of the *Lotus Sūtra*, the affairs of your entire life will be concluded. The Master said, "Is the Buddha-dharma exhausted at this point?
Is there perhaps something further beyond it? The bhikṣu marveled at his insight. They then went together to visit Xiu.
At Xianyan, the Ancient Buddha (Lingufo) said, "This youth is of the lineage of the dragon and elephant;

he shall serve as my attendant with the water-strainer and alms bowl, and in days to come, he will surely become a great vessel. The Ancient Buddha joyfully accepted him, shaved his head, and conferred upon him full ordination.

He then served alongside Master Guang of Shuangxi for seven years while attending to monastic affairs. At that time, Wansong was residing at Ba'en Temple in Yanjing, but the Master did not seek him out.
Whenever he was introduced [to others], he would invariably walk away with his arms flung out. When Song saw him, he immediately deemed him extraordinary.
For ten years, [Chang] attended him closely until he deeply grasped his essence. From then on, his reputation grew increasingly prominent, and those who followed him became ever more numerous.

Encountering the upheaval of the Renchen era, the ancestral monastery of Shaolin lay in ruins; the Emperor appointed the Master to restore it. Subsequently, Wansong Haiyun again sent a formal letter of recommendation to him.

He was summoned and subsequently accepted the invitation from Shaolin. During the time of the Shizu’s secret residence, the Emperor ordered the Master to preside over a Great Precept Assembly (*dazijie hui*).
In the year Wushen, he was summoned by imperial decree to reside at Xingguo Monastery in Helin. Before even a month had passed, the Emperor Xuanzong summoned him to his tent-palace.

His responses to the Emperor’s inquiries were to the latter's satisfaction, and he was appointed to oversee the Buddhist teachings. He restored two hundred and thirty-six abandoned monasteries for monks and nuns. In the year Gengshen, the Shizu...
The Emperor ascended the throne. Upon hearing of the debate concerning the spurious scriptures, he dispatched an official on an express courier to report the matter.

He ordered the texts to be burned and bestowed upon [Wanshou] the title "Guangzheng Bian" (Righteous Debater of the Light). He commanded that a monastery named Ba'en (Gratitude) be established in his native village, providing fields and goods to feed the monks.
At that time, there was no one capable of matching Wanshou at the monastic seat of Wan-shou. The assembly again requested that the Master take charge; when a monk asked him about the Dharma...
"What is this one path of upward nobility? The Master said, "The fisherman’s song startles the herons on the sandbar;

they fly out from the reeds, and their tracks are lost. The monk asked, "It is never hidden throughout the entire world. Where, then, is it not? Xuefeng replied, "Where is there that is not? Shishuang, for what reason, did not accord with this?
The Master said, "From of old, a filial son avoids pronouncing his father's name. A monk came to pay his respects. The Master asked, "Where are you from? The monk replied, [his origin].
[The monk from] Qingzhou said, "Do you recognize Zhaozhou’s cloth robe? [The Master] said, "Zhaozhou’s cloth robe has recently been torn by someone.
The monk asked, "Why was it torn? He replied, "Elegance does not depend on wearing many clothes. The Master then struck him.
[The monk] asked, "Why did you strike me? The Master said, "Tsk! Where is your elegance? The Master asked a monk, "The Way-source is not far;
the ocean of nature is not distant. Tell me, where is it? The monk hesitated, and the Master gave a shout.

Later, when the Master had grown old and grew weary of receiving visitors, he retired to Sōngyang. On the twentieth day of the seventh month in the autumn of the year Yihai, he manifested his passing.
He fell ill and, writing a verse, announced his passing. His secular age was seventy-three and his monastic seniority fifty-two. He was interred in a stupa at the western corner of the monastery.

Chan Master Conglun of Yanjing Ba’en Linquan first took up residence at Wanshou Monastery. Upon ascending the hall, he said: "Zen, Zen—neither orthodox nor biased; it has no path of intention, yet possesses a profound abyss.
It transcends the present and surpasses the past, outshining what comes after and illuminating what came before. One need only be able to forget one's shadow."
Traces—why must one cling to the footprints or the fishing trap? To point directly at the human mind and see one's nature, one must rely on the Patriarchal intent to penetrate the profound mystery.
The true message of nine years facing the wall: truly, within it lies a secret transmission. In the ninth year of the Zhizhi era of Emperor Yuan Shizu, he was summoned to the inner palace.
They engaged in relaxed inquiry and debate until dusk before departing. The Emperor was greatly pleased. [He] addressed the assembly: "The Northern Dipper..."
It resembles a ladle; the Southern Dipper resembles a gourd. Let it be as you please to scoop and pour. Warm sun and cool breezes;

the winter solstice and the Cold Food Festival on the one hundred and fifth day—know that the seasonal shifts do not spare anyone. Upon reaching this point, is there anyone who can swallow and spit out [the truth]? A monk asked:
"Fayan said, 'For twenty years I have understood this only as a talk about objects. Since it is not to be understood as an object, how should one understand it?"
[The Master] said: "The ape carries its young back behind the green peaks; the bird picks up fallen flowers before the azure cliffs. He addressed the assembly:
"If one discusses this matter, it is like a phoenix soaring toward the heavens, leaving no trace. This arises from the vast emptiness of nature and the brilliant clarity of the sun of wisdom.
It illuminates that the five aggregates are entirely empty, causing all manifold conditions to subside together, until one reaches the point where stars cluster in the azure void."
The moon encroaches upon the vermilion courtyard; emerald curtains hang down as candlelight wafts and people fall silent. At such a moment, how can there be room for even a breath?
How could one permit peeping or intruding? The secret chamber is not permeated by wind; the profound gate offers no foothold for the feet.
Nevertheless, a single point of numinous clarity pervades the universe; why should it be confined to West India or Caoxi? The second day of the tenth month, the eighteenth year of Zhiyuan.
On the tenth day, by imperial decree, the Daoist scriptures at Minzhong Temple in Dadu were to be burned. With the exception of the *Daode jing*, all were to be completely incinerated.
The Master was commanded to set fire to them. Ascending the seat, the Master said: "I recall in years past, during the time of Emperor Ming..."
Once, by means of a blazing fire, the beauty and ugliness [of their doctrines] were distinguished. The Son of Heaven of the Great Yuan continued the Great Plan (*Hongfan*).

Who does not know that this reveals the orthodox and crushes the heterodox? Alas! That Daoist teaching has secretly corroded Buddhist scriptures from ancient times until now, fabricating errors and forging falsehoods.

It further plunders phrases and sentences from the Śākya scriptures, plotting to inscribe its own name upon the palm-leaf manuscripts. It slanders the Tathāgata and falsely accuses the former sages; such groundless madness—
To discuss this in detail would be difficult to exhaust. It began with Zhang Ling’s fabrication of teachings that did not conform to the profound words of Laozi.

He falsely composed ritual manuals for incense offerings (*zhao*) and collated the *Lingbao* scriptures; he deceitfully claimed his Way was obtained from the void and falsely asserted it was personally transmitted by the Most High (*Taishang*).
He used the demonic arts of the Three Zhangs to delude simpletons and devised the divine talismans of the Five Movements (*wuyun shenfu*) to cast spells upon unchaste women. Ge Xiaoxian...
To search only for the essential and subtle while Tao Hongjing idly composes flowery rhetoric is no different from Du Guangting’s white-handed thievery.
Lu Xiujing’s outward kindness masking inner malice is no different from a professional persuader. Kou Qianzhi’s glib eloquence harmed others to benefit himself;
Lin Lingsu’s scheming flattery brought ruin to the state and his own family. Alas! How tragic is the fate of Fali!

Failing to meet with favor, he suffered demotion; alas, though the Way may be restored in this world, it is difficult to achieve. This has caused the sons of Śākya to grieve their hearts, yet fortunately Heaven has opened its eyes.
We reverently contemplate His Majesty, the Emperor of the Great Yuan, who expels the heterodox to return to the orthodox, and removes the false to preserve the true.

Fearing that sentient beings might fall forever into the perilous straits of delusion, and desiring that the myriad subjects may all ascend the path to enlightenment, he has therefore taken up the torch.
He drew a circle and said: "O virtuous ones, as for the sacred texts of the Three Caverns, can they still verify this Fire-Light Samādhi?
If you can understand it here, then even having the *Beidou Jing* (North Star Sutra) at home will not prevent your mouth from being restless.
If this is not yet so, then after the ashes have flown and the smoke has vanished, you may search for the Celestial Honored One wherever you go."
Look closely! When Chan Master Congkuan was nearing death, he asked his second elder brother, "The Buddhas, the Patriarchs, and my parents—I have now shot them all dead with a single arrow.
What do you think of this, Second Brother? Thereupon, he straightened his robes and passed away while seated.
Chan Master Quan-yi of Huayan Temple in Shangdu was the son of the Hao family of Xingzhou. From childhood, he was exceptionally intelligent, surpassing other children.

At the age of six, he shaved his head and went to attend upon Wansong. Possessing a vast memory and extensive learning, his discourse and debate were unimpeded. Wansong appointed him as his attendant.
Whenever he heard a verse, eulogy, or dharma talk from Wansong, he understood it immediately; thus, he received the Dharma. He served constantly as an attendant.

His responses were timely and his spiritual acumen was unassailable. Liu Bingzhong, the Grand Guardian (Taibao), recommended that the Master was of great utility. Emperor Shizu summoned him for an audience; after conversing with him, the Emperor was greatly pleased.

He remained at the royal court, offering much counsel and benefit. After three years, he was released and returned home, whereupon the Emperor bestowed upon him the title of Great Chan Master Foguo Puan.
In the fifth month of the Dingmao year of the Zhizheng era, he manifested illness and passed away lying on his right side. It was extraordinary.
The incense burned for three days, and the *śarīra* relics were innumerable.
The Chancellor Yelü Zhinqing, a lay practitioner (*upāsaka*) whose courtesy name was Chucái, was originally surnamed Yelü.

When the Jin dynasty extinguished the Liao, he returned to the Jin and changed his surname to Yelü. Initially, while in the capital, the Master saw many eminent Chan masters, yet he revered only [the Master] Sheng.
Master An-cheng frequently visited him to inquire about the Way of the Patriarchs, repeatedly testing him with passages he had obtained from the recorded sayings of ancient and eminent masters.

On several occasions, Sheng’an granted his approval, leading the Master to believe he had attained realization. However, since he encountered personal calamities and afflictions, [his understanding has changed].
His ambition for fame and office was confined to a high tower, yet his search for the Way of the Patriarchs grew ever more urgent.

He subsequently revisited Sheng’an with the same questions as before, but Sheng’an overturned his previous case and did not agree with what he had seen. The Master was greatly perplexed. Sheng’an spoke to him calmly, saying:
In the past, you occupied a position of importance, and moreover, many Confucian scholars did not truly believe in Buddhist scriptures;
they merely plucked out phrases and anecdotes to serve as material for conversation. Therefore, I did not dare to exert myself in providing rigorous correction.
Now, however, I judge that your heart is indeed seeking the fundamental matter in questioning me; how could I still persist in my former faults and fail to provide rigorous correction? I am old.
There was an elder named Wansong, who was fully accomplished in both Confucianism and Buddhism and proficient in both the Chan school and the scriptural teachings.

His eloquence was unimpeded; you may see for yourself his public records. Having entered the study under Wansong, he cut off all human contact and set aside all domestic affairs. Whether in bitter cold or humid heat, there was not a day that he did not attend to his practice.
Burning oil lamps to extend the light of day, he neglected sleep and forgot to eat for nearly three years, until he finally attained certification. He was titled...
The layman Zhanran, in his preface evaluating the ancients, stated briefly: "The Buddhas, patriarchs, and various masters have their roots buried ten fathoms deep;
the hundred cases of karmic conditions sprout shoots upon being seen in this world. Tiantong ought not to have pulled up the branches, and Wansong could hardly be expected to lead out the vines.
Zhanran, however, adds further thorny ropes to those very branches and vines, piercing the nostrils of those who merely follow scents and pursue fragrances, and tripping up those who..."
The marvelous root of the profound essence: if you wish to have your heels touch the ground and your nostrils reach toward heaven, you must first pass through this tangle of complications.

Previously, when the Great Sovereign was about to campaign westward, the officials submitted a memorial stating that among the monks of Wutai and other regions, those who possessed incantatory arts, military strategy, or physical prowess could be recruited for the expeditionary forces.

As the troops were following him on a western expedition, the Master stopped them, saying: "The eminent practitioners of the Śākya school must strictly observe the precept against killing and uphold the practice of compassion and patience.
Thus, there are those who would rather endanger their own lives than take the life of a goose for its pearl, and those who would rather die than pull up a living blade of grass.
The laws of the Dharma King are to be reverently followed; even at the cost of death, one must not transgress them. How could it be appropriate to employ such people as soldiers? His...

"One who does not follow the laws and regulations will surely lack purposeful conduct. Since he has already violated the Buddha’s intent there, how could he possibly be loyal to the King’s service here?
Therefore, none of them may follow the Imperial Preceptor. The Emperor followed this advice. The Master passed away in the sixteenth year of Taizong’s reign.
He lived to the age of fifty-five (which was the third year of the Chunyu era of the Southern Song dynasty).
He was the twenty-fourth generation descendant of Qingyuan and the dharma heir of Chan Master Shaoshi Yu.
The Chan Master Wentai of Lingyin on Mount Shaoshi in the Western Capital (Luoyang) was of unknown lineage.

His intelligence and insight surpassed those of others, and he was deeply devoted to the *zongcheng* (the vehicle of the school). He traveled to Mount Shaoshi, where before long he realized the essential point of the mind.

Thus, among those of that time who were called the "two Taís and one Sù"—the eminent disciples of Xueting—he was one of them. Ascending the hall, he said: "Matters from kalpas as numerous as motes of dust are present right here."
Now, the wondrous virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are all within the source of the mind. Try having him present them face-to-face;
he will not know how to bring them forth against the wind. Tell me, where does the fault lie? He plants his staff and says: "It is precisely because they are too clear."
On the contrary, it causes what is attained to be delayed.
Chan Master Zhitaí of Zhōnglín at Bào’ēn Monastery in Tàiyuán was the son of the Wēn family of Yúchéng in Fényáng.
He shaved his hair at Huáyán Monastery and sighed deeply, saying: "A great man ought to investigate the Great Matter; how can he occupy himself with such trivialities?"
At that time, Master Wanshou was at Xueting; the Master went to rely upon him for several years, attaining a realization that was transcendent.

The imperial court took note of the Master’s reputation and issued a decree for him to reside at Baoen Monastery. A monk asked, "What is it like where there is not a single inch of grass for ten thousand miles?
The Master said, "This is not a realm for you, O Layman (Ajari), to tread upon. The monk asked, "What is it like when one steps out the door and there is grass everywhere? The Master said:
"As soon as one moves, it is already contrary [to the truth]. He asked, "How is it that not leaving the gate is also a vast expanse of weeds?

The Master said, "To dwell upon it is an error. He asked, "How can one avoid being involved in movement and stillness? The Master said, "The entire realm is devoid of red dust; the whole body is without reflection.
One day, manifesting illness, he gathered the assembly for final instructions, wrote a verse, and passed away.
Chan Master Jingxu of Zuanan at Lingyan in Taian Prefecture was a native of Yongping in Baoding.

His clan name was Zhang. He took Shousheng of Xiangshan as his teacher and engaged in formal study for over ten years. During this time, he encountered more than ten spiritual mentors (*jñāna-kalyāṇamitra*).
Finally, he visited Xueting at Wanshou Monastery; after several years of refinement and training, Xueting bestowed upon him the robe and verse of transmission. Initially, he presided over...
Longevity! Next, at Lingyan on Shaoshi Mountain, he ascended the hall and said: "The white dew stretches across the river; yellow chrysanthemums fill the garden.
The sound of the mortar strikes through the night moon; the crickets wail in the autumn wind. Cicadas chirp in the trees by the bank;
leaves part from the branches beyond the railing. Every color manifests the Sea-Seal Samādhi; every sound turns the fundamental Dharma wheel. If you all can realize this..."
If you attain it, it is like facing a mirror where the eyebrows and eyes are clearly distinct; only then can you be called half a monk.
Yet, there is still worldly air that has not been removed. If you could break the mirror, then I would truly be able to meet you.
But as for what happens after we have met—there are thirty more blows! Wait until another time. Later, he retired to Xiangshan.
One day, he gathered the assembly to take his leave and passed away while lying on his right side.
He was the Dharma successor of Chan Master Shaoshi Tai of the twenty-fifth generation after Qingyuan.
Chan Master Huan-yuan Fuyu of Bao-ying Monastery in the Western Capital was a native of the Wang family in Ling-shi, Huo Prefecture.

He received the tonsure at Doushuai Monastery in his home district and traveled extensively among the lecture halls, where his eloquence flowed like a stream. Later, hearing that Chan Master Lingyin possessed the perfectly clear eye of the Way, he devoted himself to him for investigation and study.
One day, while listening to Lingyin’s ascent to the hall, he heard [the Master] cite: "One must absolutely not seek it from others; far away..."
He spoke to him in informal, colloquial language. The Master immediately attained sudden realization and was granted formal approval (*kanna*).
He first resided at Tianqing and subsequently at Baoying. A monk asked, "What is the great meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?

The Master said, "The wind carries the sound of the spring to my pillow; the moon shifts the shadows of the flowers to my window. The monk asked, "What is the Prince at birth? The Master said, "Although he exists..."
[The questioner asked: "What is the portion of nobility? [The Master replied: "One who is not a noble person. [The questioner asked: "What is a prince born at dawn? The Master said:
"Though he ascends the golden register of honor, in the end he remains but an old court official. [The questioner asked: "What is a prince born at twilight? The Master said:
"Only after enduring every hardship does one finally behold the sky of Yao. [The questioner asked: "What is a prince born by transformation? The Master said: "He is like a father..."

There was no difference in his essence. Temporarily exercising authority over the affairs beyond the palace gates, he asked: "What is the Prince born within? The Master said: "He has always resided deep within the palace;
though but a few inches away, he is close to the Dragon’s countenance. He asked: "Please, Master, point out the path that leads upward.

The Master said: "The stringless lute has its melody; how could humans or devas hear it? He passed away at the end of the tenth month of the Gui-chou year of Huangqing (1313), at the age of sixty-nine.
The forty-ninth day of the lunar year.

Chan Master Yueyan Yongda of Baoying Temple in the Western Capital was a dharma successor of Chan Master Lingyan Su. He was the son of the Liu family of Fenyang and received the tonsure in his native prefecture.

At Tianning Temple, he constantly exhorted himself with the reality of birth and death. Hearing that the Dharma-thunder of Lingyan resounded afar during his southern pilgrimage, he longed for its wind-like virtue from afar and traveled there on foot to seek instruction.
Upon meeting him, Lingyan recognized his potential; after a long period of close study, he finally entered the profound depths of the teaching.
He then declared: "Realization depends upon the teacher, but practice rests with oneself. Thereupon, he went to AnTaizhou to enter a retreat. After a long time, both monastics and laypeople...
He was firmly entreated to remain at Baoying, and having no choice, he arose. He ascended the hall and said:
"The old man of Lukmon said, 'The entire earth is the student’s single volume of scripture; the entire universe is the student’s single eye.
To view this scripture with this eye, there shall be no interruption for ten million billion kalpas. Later, the old man Wansong truly reached the end of his resources."
My strength is exhausted. I say: "To read and contemplate this is no easy task. Can you all read and contemplate it? You must know that who among you does not possess this single volume of scripture?
Who among you does not have this one eye perfectly round? If you wish for it to be long, it is inexhaustible throughout billions of kalpas;
if you wish for it to be short, it is complete in a single kṣaṇa. Today, Baoying does not spare his eyebrows to [explain it] for you.
The assembly pointed their fingers. He then snapped his fingers once and said, "Look! You have read it. Do not let this pass you by. After a long silence, he struck his whisk and said:
"From this point on, there is no returning; should one return, it can be attained. Who else would vie for the misty scenery of the Five Lakes?"
One day, he manifested illness and passed away peacefully.
The Chan Master Pujiu of Fenglong Mountain’s ancient cliff was born into the Liu clan of Huyang. At the age of fifteen, he went to Chanqing Monastery to leave the household life and visited Lingyan.
There, Lingyan subjected him to further refinement with the hammer and tongs of his fundamental teaching; his doubts were suddenly shattered like an explosion.
[The transmission] was passed down. In the sixth year of the Dading era, Chan Master Yue’an Hai retired from his seat. The monastery prepared a formal petition to invite the Master to open the hall.
By imperial decree, he was granted the title Great Chan Master Miaoyan Hongfa. Shortly thereafter, he received an invitation from Longjian, which he accepted with some reluctance.
A monk asked, "What is the 'falling of the skull'? The Master said, "It is not one who wears fur and horns. [The monk asked,] "What is the 'following'?"
"Fallen," the Master said. "This is not one who hears sounds or sees forms. The monk asked, "What is 'the noble fall'? The Master said, "This is not one who cuts off sound and form.
The monk asked, "If that is so, how can it be called a 'fall'? The Master said, "A wild goose flies across the vast sky; its shadow sinks into the cold water.

The monk asked, "The ancients said that these three falls are the sickness of those who have finished their business. If they are people who have finished their business, why would they have such sickness?"
"How is it that you have this illness? The Master said, "It is simply because of attending to affairs that the illness arises.
[The monk] asked, "When will this illness be cured? The Master said, "Wait until there is no body; then this illness will be eliminated. Thereupon, he presented this verse:

"The heavy golden locks have long since been flung open; Tranquil and at ease, I go and come alone through the three realms. A wild goose passes through the vast sky, leaving no trace; Its reflection sinks into the cold water."
"Let him speculate as he will. Later, he returned to live in seclusion at Lingqi. Not long after, he manifested his passing. His worldly age was seventy-seven.
He was a Dharma successor of Chan Master Baoying Yu of the twenty-sixth generation under Qingyuan.
Chan Master Xiangyan Chunzhu Wencai of Dengzhou was the son of the Yao family of Linfen in Pingyang. From birth, he possessed extraordinary qualities;

whenever he saw a monk, he would join his palms and prostrate himself, differing from ordinary children. When grown, he relied upon Master Fuyuan Puguang of Mingfu Monastery in Jiangzhou to leave the household life.
Once, while reading the *Song of Realizing the Way*, he reached the line, "The illusory, empty body is itself the Dharma-body," and attained a joyful realization.
Wu went to visit Master Huan-yuan to present his understanding. Huan-yuan approved it. He spent three years reading the Tripitaka at Longmen Mountain.

In the Jiazi year of the Taiding era, he resided at Shaoshi, and subsequently lived in seclusion at Xiangyan. There, he provided commentaries on the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra* and the *Huayan fajie guan*.
A monk asked, "What is the realm of principle? The Master said, "The void falls to the ground, and its powder..."

[The questioner’s words] were fragmented and did not form a coherent text. [The questioner] asked: "What is the phenomenal dharma-realm (*vastu-dharmadhātu*)? The Master said: "When you arrive, the house is utterly emptied; thus one avoids being a fool within the dwelling. [The questioner] asked:

"What is the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between phenomena and principle (*vastu-tattva-avyāghāta-dharmadhātu*)? The Master said: "In the depths of winter, the withered tree puts forth its brilliance."
In the ninth month of summer, snowflakes flew. [A disciple] asked, "What is the Dharma-realm of unimpededness in all things?

The Master replied, "The clear breeze accompanies the bright moon; the rustic elder smiles as they draw near. On the seventeenth day of the fifth month of the Renchen year of the Zhizheng era, he bathed, changed his robes, and summoned his disciples to deliver his final instructions.
He said, "When I die, there is no need for the wasteful expenditure of funeral rites. Once the fire has risen, scattering my ashes will suffice."
The following day, he passed away with auspicious signs. His entire body was interred in the Snow Court Pagoda (Seongjeong-tap) to the right. He was eighty years of age.
Seon Master Yeokam Jeol was the dharma heir of Seon Master Yunhyeon Do-seong of Cheonjae Temple in Gimjeong, who was a distant descendant of King Taejo of the Goryeo dynasty. [His father...]
He moved his residence to Baoding and settled there. At the age of fifteen, he left the household life at Xingguo Temple in the commandery.
The Master had a broad forehead and a flat brow, with a majestic and imposing presence; he possessed great ambition.

After receiving full ordination, he formed a group of three companions and dwelt in an earthen cave in Qingzhou, where they secretly investigated the essence of the Single Transmission. Suddenly, an old man of remarkably ancient appearance appeared and said to him: "You..."

"These three men have forgotten bitterness and toil; through their simple and pure practice, they have investigated and clarified the great matter that transcends the ordinary. In days to come, they will surely become pillars of the Dharma-gate.

The Master rebuked him, saying, "If they are to be pillars of the Dharma, why do they dwell within earthen caves? The old man replied: [The text here implies the Master's words were met with a challenge or a counter-argument regarding the nature of practice].
"There has never been one who acts constantly without abiding, nor one who abides constantly without acting. Having finished speaking, he vanished.
The Master redoubled his diligent efforts in secret. Later, hearing that Master Jie of Qiujiang was widely propagating the principles of Caodong at Lingyan, he went there to pay his respects.
Jie asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "From Qingzhou. Jie said, "Did you bring the Qingzhou cloth robe with you?"
"Ma? The Master said, "I have presented it to the Abbot. Jie said, "Go to the hall for meditation. After some time, his long-standing doubts were suddenly and completely resolved.
He went straight to the master’s quarters. Jie asked, "Has the golden lock and mysterious gate been opened yet?
The Master replied, "What old kernel are you looking for inside a thousand-year-old peach pit? Jie nodded in approval and instructed him, saying, "This is what you originally possess."
"In matters of practice, you have well protected and maintained yourself. One day, it will surely be you who can propagate my Way. The Master returned to Qingzhou.
The assembly requested that he reside at Dazeshan in Donglai. Subsequently, he resided at Puzhao.

In the fifteenth year of the Hongwu era, the Sangsi (Buddhist Administration) was established in all prefectures and counties to oversee the teachings of Śākyamuni. The Master was selected for this office; his Way accorded with the profound favor of the Prince.

He was treated with exceptional honor. In the eighth month of the autumn of the thirtieth year, the Emperor summoned the Master to the palace and commanded him to reside at Tien-chiai (Heavenly Realm) Monastery.
The Master submitted a petition stating that he did not understand the Buddha-dharma. The Emperor then composed a poem, engraved upon a golden plaque and hung in the Dharma Hall, which reads:

"He declined my words; I permitted his silence. The single sandal returning west is the ancient direct transmission. At the empty King’s Hall, drums and bells ring out on the first and fifteenth days."
Pointing to his seat, he said: "Counting back from years past, I ascend the hall. Ten thousand acres of white clouds roll and unfurl, revealing the true mechanism beyond kalpas;

a thousand peaks of crimson leaves blaze forth, manifesting the wondrous intent within this very moment. Unfailing throughout antiquity and the present, it remains ever-present through dust-like eons.
The bird-path is empty yet permeable as one sets foot upon it; the profound gate is subtle and dense. The lion’s string vibrates as the fingers press its chords—this is the ancient [Way]."

The resonance is resonant and rhythmic; it is enough to make the stone woman nod her head and the wooden man clap his hands. Grasping the golden needle and jade thread, one pierces through the point prior to the mechanism.
Cutting off the hare’s horn and tortoise hair, one illuminates the upward direction and the primary and secondary deviations. It is revealed alone, encompassing both the hidden and the manifest.
Thus, in every object, at every head, in every speck of dust and every world-system, there is not even a single hair’s breadth lacking. Great Assembly!
Do you understand? Last night a wooden horse passed through the clouds; it startled the Southern and Northern Dipper constellations into hiding.

In the tenth month of that year, by imperial decree, a Great Universal Salvation Retreat (Pudu Dazhai) was established at the temple for three days and nights. The Emperor personally led the hundred officials to perform the sacrificial rites.

Once the offerings were presented, he visited the abbot’s quarters and engaged in leisurely conversation. He bestowed several *ding* of precious paper currency (*baocao*). [The Master] ascended the hall. [The discourse on] the Yin...
The extreme yang returns and transforms as the days grow long; plum blossoms everywhere emit their fragrant scent.

Within this, there is not much of a secret to be found—how could it ever be hidden throughout the entire realm? Thus, in this clear and manifest state, one encounters it at the tips of a hundred blades of grass;
it is secretly proclaimed within the radiance of the ten thousand phenomena. On the field of profit and fame, recognize the Unranked True Person. The person...

In the mountains, I manifest my original face; its reflection contains the mirror of the school. When the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise; the body is the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
When the mind ceases, all manner of phenomena cease. The barren woman holds aloft the precious seal, its patterns fully revealed;
the wooden man silently passes through the golden shuttle, not missing a single hair’s breadth. He pulls the mechanism of the wheel beyond the kalpas, blazing brilliantly throughout the world.

The sun and moon within the center penetrate far and near; they cause even withered wood to bloom with flowers. Encompassing all that is ancient and modern, they enable cold ashes to burst into flame.
Clouds shroud the ancient path, where the lingering colors of the wilds still bewilder; the moon fills the cold crags, its brilliant divine light shining everywhere.
When the mechanisms of the six gates have ceased, there is no need for circuitous or indirect inquiry; when the function of the single color is perfected, one must strictly avoid facing it directly.

The seal on the head is broken. The white ox treading its path has already received the conditions for building and transforming; the jade horse neighing in the wind is entirely a matter of benefiting sentient beings.
But tell me, what is the matter that transcends this? *Pfft!* A staff of rabbit horns picks up the moon at the bottom of the pond;
a whisk of tortoise hair hangs from the clouds atop the ridge. [Ascending the hall: When the three yang lines intersect in harmony, all things are renewed. To manifest the One True...
This wondrous function is the profound source of all transformation; in every atom it merges with the Way, and at every place there is a passage to the ford.

The Dharma assembly is grandly inaugurated and the Garden of Enlightenment is widely opened. The destiny of the nation flourishes in tandem with the destiny of the Buddha, and the imperial wind blows alongside the wind of the school.
Just as it is said that the old year has passed and the new year has arrived, I do not know where that which departs goes to, nor from where that which comes arrives. As for this—

This commentary is increasingly seen as contradictory and erroneous. I venture to ask the assembly: within the single stroke beneath the patched robe, is there still any coming or going, any increase or decrease?
If you can realize this, you will see that when the year ends, the harmony of the Yanghe wind brings forth the shadowless tree;

when spring returns, flowers bloom upon the sproutless branch. Entering the hall, he said: "In the fifth month, the hibiscus flowers shine brightly before the eyes; the fragrant breeze and warbling birds pervade the crags."
The bolt [of the gate]. One move ahead of the mechanism contains no mystery or subtlety. One must strictly avoid identifying with form and sound.
Remember that when Master Chan Heshang Jia Shan addressed the assembly, he said: "There is no dharma before the eyes; the intent lies before the eyes.
It is not a dharma of the present moment; it is beyond what the ears and eyes can reach. Tiantong Ju said: "Old man Jia Shan untied the sack and brought forth rare treasures."
The jewels have been scattered before all the people. At such a time as this, what further is there to do? "The traveler does not pick up what is lost"—this is praised by the gentlemen.
O Great Assembly, if one examines the views of these two masters, Jiashan and Tiantong, one after another, they are both found to be full of leaks and flaws.
Fengshan’s own position is not like this; if it were a matter of seeing through form...
Seeking through sound is not the treasure of the home. To realize that not a single dharma exists before one’s eyes, every head and every object is in total resonance.
Should this not yet be so, listen further to the final phrase: "When the Way prevails, the Son of Heaven does not issue commands;
when the times are clear, there is no need to sing songs of peace. On the seventh month of the thirty-fifth year, Emperor Taizong Wen succeeded to the precious throne.

He was dispatched as an envoy to the Kingdom of Japan to proclaim the sacred transformation [of the Dharma]. He returned in the second year and submitted a detailed report together with his fellow officials and subordinates;

the Emperor’s heart was greatly pleased, and the favor bestowed upon him exceeded all previous honors. In the fourth year, due to the slander of his subordinates, he was imprisoned for over a hundred days.
The Master remained composed and free from anxiety. The Sovereign, recognizing that he was innocent, granted him amnesty. In the spring of the sixth year, by imperial decree:
At Zhongshan, he established a Great Universal Deliverance Retreat (Pudu Dazhai) and commissioned the Master to preach the Dharma; those who listened numbered in the tens of thousands.
In the eleventh year, he traveled to Beijing for the New Year’s audience and, by imperial decree, conducted a retreat at Qingshou Monastery, receiving exceptional gifts and honors.

In the third year of Xuande, when the Master was seventy-six years old, he submitted a memorial requesting to return to the mountains. Emperor Xuanzong, out of compassion for his sincerity, dispatched—

The inner court officials escorted him back south to the West Hermitage of Cheonjae Temple to spend his final years there. On the eighth day of the twelfth month of the seventh year, he manifested slight illness;

bidding farewell to the assembly, he spoke a verse and passed away while sitting in the lotus posture. The Sovereign dispatched an official to offer a sacrificial rite accompanied by a written inscription.
He was eighty-one years of age and had sixty-five years of monastic seniority (*śrāmaṇera*). On the day of his cremation, the smoke and flames were of five colors, and immortal cranes soared above.
The air was filled with a wondrous, ethereal fragrance. Over ten thousand people, including officials and the fourfold assembly, all marveled at such a rare occurrence.
After the cremation, countless round, red-colored śarīras were collected. A stūpa was erected outside the Ande Gate of Yingten City.
By imperial decree, the site of the stūpa was granted the name Juefeng Chan Temple.

Chan Master Xianan Yirang of Tianqing Temple in the Western Capital was a dharma successor of Chan Master Fenglong Jiu. A native of the Li clan from Zhending, he shaved his head and donned the robes at the age of seven, traveling to consult various patriarchs of the school.
