The Emperor was greatly pleased and conferred upon him the title of Grand Master Guanghui Yuanwu. After the Master had rebuilt Longxiang and its construction was just completed, he passed away.
He was a Dharma successor of Chan Master Fu of Mount Jing.
Chan Master Yue Nan-chu of Mount Jing, Hangzhou, was a native of Longxing. He ascended the hall and said: "Awakening to the Way through sound;
clarifying the mind through form. Suddenly picking up his staff, he said, "This is form," and striking it once, he said, "This is sound."
Everyone sees and hears this together. But which is the luminous mind? Which is the path of awakening? He let out a shout and said:
"To covet another's single grain of rice, one loses six months' worth of provisions. He was posthumously titled Chan Master Foci Faxi.
Chan Master Huizhong Haixin of Tianjie Monastery in Nanjing was a dharma successor of Chan Master Tantan of Tiandong. He was the son of the Jiang family of Fenghua.

At the age of fifteen, he went to Fahua Temple to leave the household life. Thereafter, he shaved his head, received full ordination, and studied the teachings, learning the principles of the Three Contemplations (*sanguan*). Later...
He went to visit Zhuxi. Zhuxi, knowing him to be a vessel for the Dharma, treated him with a stern countenance and would not exchange a single word with him.
The Master’s doubts grew ever more intense. One day, as Zhuxi ascended the hall, he raised the story of Xinghua striking Kebin and questioned the Master about it.

The Master replied, "How magnificent! A lion cub indeed. Zhuxi nodded his head in approval, and the Master then remained in attendance under him. He served through various offices until he reached the position of Librarian. In the year of Bingyin, the Tai Ding era, he departed.

The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara appeared to him while he was dwelling in clarity. On Mount Potalaka, he was bestowed with the title "Chan Master Hongjiao, Bestower of the Treasure of Wisdom through Vast Intelligence and Sublime Enlightenment," along with a set of dharma robes.
In the *Renwu* year of the *Zhizheng* era, he ascended to Upper Zhong; in the *Yiyou* year, he ascended to Tiantong.

In the tenth month of winter, he moved to serve as the abbot of Longxiang. When the Ming army descended upon Jinling, the temple monks dispersed, but the Master alone sat in meditative posture (*paryaṅka*). He held...
Soldiers lined the way before him, all of whom cast down their weapons and prostrated themselves. Emperor Gao once visited his temple and listened to the Master’s exposition of the Dharma;
admiring the Master’s pure and sincere conduct and speech, he specifically renamed Longxiang Monastery "Great Tianjie" and bestowed exceptional honors upon him.
One day he said to those around him, "I am about to depart. You should all take it upon yourselves to uphold the Dharma and strive with diligent energy.
Having finished speaking, he passed away. His attendant requested that he leave behind a verse, whereupon he took up his brush and wrote:
"A lifetime spent in accordance with the Way; Seventy-eight years of letting it flow forth. This morning, casting off my hands, I go; Ten thousand miles of clear, empty sky."
A single snowflake fell. Having finished writing, he closed his eyes again. His remains stayed in the stupa for seven days, his countenance appearing as if alive.
On the day before his passing, the Emperor was supervising military operations in Jiangyin and dreamed that the Master came to pay him a visit. The Emperor asked, "Why have you come, Master?

The Master replied, "I am about to return to the West and have come to bid you farewell. When the imperial carriage returned to Jinling, the report of the Master's death arrived; it coincided exactly with the dream.
The Emperor was struck with wonder and issued an imperial decree from the inner treasury to assist with the funeral arrangements.

On the evening the coffin was lifted, the Emperor personally presented offerings and escorted it beyond the capital gates. It was cremated before Mount Zubao, where śarīra relics appeared in quantities like hemp seeds and beans.

The five colors were brilliantly radiant, and wherever the smoke reached, there too they appeared in dense clusters. The master’s disciple Sengsheng divined a site on the eastern foot of Mount Niushou and constructed a stupa there.
Chan Master Jiefeng Shiyu of Wushan Mountain in Quzhou was a dharma heir of Chan Master Dachicheng. He was the son of the Yu family from Xian County in the prefecture.

He entered the monastic order at Xianjiao Monastery in Lanxi. After receiving full ordination, he traveled extensively to visit various spiritual teachers (*jñānin*), yet he found no point of entry. Later, he visited Zhiyan.

He was instructed to contemplate that it is "neither mind, nor Buddha, nor a thing. One night, he sat in meditation until the late hours when he heard a neighboring monk recite the *Zhengdao ge* (Song of Realizing the Way), which says:
"Do not eliminate delusive thoughts; do not seek the truth. At once, he felt as though a heavy burden had been lifted from his shoulders. He then composed this verse:
From time to time we meet face-to-face, yet do not truly encounter one another; having exhausted the vital energy of one’s mother, one reaches the end of strength.
At midnight, suddenly forgetting the pointing finger of the moon, the red solar disc bursts forth from the void. He went to see Yanguan, who said, "Where have you come from seeing gods and ghosts?"
The Master said, "I have caught the thief. Yankou asked, "Where is the stolen goods? The Master gave a shout. Yankou said, "Neither opening the mouth nor closing the mouth is right.
Speak one word that goes beyond this! The Master said, "Clearly manifest throughout the entire world, nothing is concealed.
Yankou raised his bamboo staff and said, "To call it a bamboo staff is to encounter resistance; not to call it a bamboo staff is to turn one's back."

"What is your name? The Master then overturned the meditation seat. Yunyan struck him with his bamboo staff three times, saying, "You blind fellow, how dare you come here to pull at a tiger's whiskers!
The Master then bowed. He went to see Yuangong, who asked, "Where have you come from?
The Master replied, "From Daci. Yuangong asked, "How deep is the nostril of Daci? The Master tapped the ground once with his staff. Yuangong said:
"Breaking off the staff, what will you strike with? The Master then prostrated and said, "Today I have personally seen the Elder.
The Elder said, "Out of consideration for you, disciple and grandson, I shall let you off thirty blows. He returned to Daci and served there for three years.
One day, Yan said to the Master, "The ancients sought teachers and chose friends; one must not squander or lose their precious time. Although you have attained Buddhahood..."
The Patriarch’s Way of responding to transformations had not yet allowed him to turn his body upward; thus, he cited the story of Fengyang seeing Shoushan:
"The moon in the empty realm of the ten-thousand-year-old green pool—only after repeated scooping and stirring does one finally come to know it. At this, the Master attained great enlightenment.
He returned to Wushan in Xian’an, where he built a thatched hut to dwell. Gradually, it became a monastic center, attracting a community of three thousand followers. (Year 6 of Zhizheng)
He resided at Shixi for many years. A monk asked, "Having left far behind Mount Wushi, you come to dwell on Stone Creek Mountain.

You reveal the path for humans and devas; how does one penetrate the Patriarch’s barrier? The Master said, "A dragon gives birth to a golden phoenix chick, which pierces through the azure lapis lazuli.

The monk said, "If it is so, then face-to-face we do not recognize each other, yet from a thousand miles away we share the same wind. The Master said, "Layer upon layer are the mountain passes and roads. The monk said, [and remained silent].
“Bodhidharma came from the West not to establish written words, but to point directly to the human mind, so that one may see one’s nature and become a Buddha.

Since he did not establish written words, how is it that they have been transmitted down to the present day? The Master said, “In official matters, even a needle is not permitted; yet in private affairs, carts and horses pass through.

[The student] asked, “When you say ‘pointing directly to the human mind,’ what mind do you point to? The Master said, “When the mouth opens, it is not on the tongue. [The student] asked, “Regarding ‘seeing one’s nature and becoming a Buddha’...”
"Where does Buddha-nature reside? The Master said, "The Taihu Lake spans thirty-six thousand acres; night after night, the moonlight shines bright upon its waves.
A questioner asked, "When the flower blossomed at the Huangmei mortar, the robe was passed at midnight to Lingnan.
Is this matter truly so, or not? The Master said, "Originally there is not a single thing; one's two shoulders cannot bear it. The questioner said, "It is not the wind..."
"Movement is not the movement of the banner; it is the mind of the worthy one that moves. [The monk] asked, "How about this?
The Master said, "To know that the lamp is fundamentally fire; to believe that water does not depart from the waves. [The monk] asked, "And how is the Master’s single phrase for the sake of others?
The Master said, "A slap across the face; a blow behind the head. [The monk] said, "In that case, it is the heart of a grandmother in its urgency. The Master said, "Not from the great surging waves."
Casting fragrant bait, one strives to catch the golden-scaled fish upon the fishing boat. Entering the hall, [the Master said]: "A single blow struck atop a ten-thousand-fathom peak;
body ground to powder, head shattered, all doubt and suspicion vanish. Suddenly, after death, one revives once more, and the myriad phenomena and the host of beings open their laughing eyes."
Tell me, what is he laughing at? This time, having recognized the path from whence one comes, one shall no longer enter a mother’s womb. (He lets out a shout.
For the most part, when Master An came to attend upon him, the Master asked, "Master Lecturer, what sutra do you lecture?
He replied, "The Diamond Sutra. I have attained a place of realization in the state where there is nowhere from which one comes and nowhere to which one goes. The Master said, "Since..."
"How is it that you have arrived here despite having neither come nor gone? The Master said, "It is precisely this state of neither coming nor going.
The Master asked, "Where are you right now? The host gave a shout. The Master said, "Stop for a moment with that shout and your fist.
When the four elements disperse, where will you establish yourself and sustain your life? The host replied, "Throughout the entire earth, where is there that is not oneself?"
[The monk] said, "If one suddenly encounters the kalpa-fire blazing forth and the great trichiliocosm is utterly destroyed, what then?
The Master said, "At this point, I do not understand. The Master said, "The Sixth Patriarch did not understand; he split wood and pounded rice. Bodhidharma did not recognize [his own nature];
he sat facing the wall for nine years. What have you seen that you do not understand? [The monk] said, "I simply do not understand. The Master said, "Blind fellow! Please [speak further]."
He sat and drank tea. In the twelfth month of the third year of the Hongwu era, he manifested a slight illness. He wrote a verse, saying: "Birth is fundamentally not born;
cessation is fundamentally not ceased. Casting off my hands, I go forth; the sky is filled with the bright moon. Having thrown down his brush, he passed away.
His disciples enshrined his entire body in the Chiyun Pagoda Courtyard.
Chan Master Niche Creek Zhishun of Xuefeng in Fuzhou was a successor of Chan Master Tianbao Shu. He was a native of the Chen family in Ruian, Wenzhou.

He left home at the age of seven and received full ordination. He subsequently entered Min Province to visit Tieguan, who transmitted to him the essentials of the mind. After more than a month, while he was using the toilet—
Seeing a bottle gourd in the garden, he attained a realization. He presented what he had awakened to in order to seek verification.

Guankui said, "This is merely entering the gate; the Supreme Vehicle is still very far away. He then instructed him, saying, "You must completely discard your previous understandings and exert yourself solely in the practice of *can* (investigation) and *ti* (raising the question).
Then you will naturally enter the innermost depths. One day, while Guankui was about to give an evening sermon, [Zhaozhou] intended to leave his mat. Suddenly—
Huo’an said to Guankou, “I have now seen the point where Nanquan failed. Guankou asked, “It is not mind, it is not Buddha, and it is not an object;
what is it? The Master replied, “The ground is paved with bricks, and the roof is covered with tiles. Guankou said, “So it is.”
"Where is Nanquan right now? The Master said, "A hawk has flown to Silla. Guankai said, "Wrong. The Master also said, "Wrong.
Guankai said, "Wrong, wrong! The Master performed a single prostration. Guankai assembled the assembly to examine him.
The Master laughed and said, "Before a word was uttered, we were already not involved with one another. Where, then, is the Master’s eye? Furthermore, this has become a mere theatrical performance."

Yeguan said, "I must ensure that everyone knows. He then questioned the Master on each of the essential sayings of the Chan school one by one. The Master answered them all completely, and Yeguan approved.

He subsequently appointed him to manage the treasury keys and soon after ordered him to share the teaching seat. When Yeguan passed away, the assembly requested him to succeed to the position and continue presiding over Baen Temple.
He later moved back to his original residence, where the imperial court bestowed upon him a Dharma robe and the posthumous title "Buddha-nature Perfectly Discerning."

After some time, he distributed all his robes and alms-bowl stores among others and retired to a single room. He dug into the earth to make a hearth and broke bamboo to fashion chopsticks, living with utter simplicity.
When the Chancellor Yan Zhibuhua was dispatched to govern the province of Min, he invited the Master to reside at Dongchan Monastery.
In less than a year, he reformed the old and established the new as if by divine creation; even upon ascending Xuefeng, he rectified its decay.
At the beginning of the Hongwu era, an imperial edict summoned ten monks of realized virtue to Mount Zhongshan to establish an Unrestricted Dharma Assembly (*mochae*).

The Master ascended the seat to preach the Dharma in accordance with the decree. The Imperial Carriage visited in person, and the Emperor’s inquiries and consolations were most thorough. Returning south, he resided at Jingci Temple. Just then—
By imperial decree, virtuous śramaṇas were summoned to the capital to serve as advisors. The assembly unanimously recommended the Master to the capital.

After four months had passed, on the first day of the month, he requested a bath, wrote a verse of farewell, and passed away. Through cremation, countless śarīras were obtained; these were taken back and used to construct a stūpa.
Chan Master Wumen Cong of Xiangshan in Ruzhou was a successor of Chan Master Tie-shan Qiong.
A native of Xiangshan, he first studied under Dugu Weng, who instructed him to investigate the koan of the "Three Not-sos.
He did not yet achieve awakening. One day, the senior monk Jing said to him, "If you wish to know the ultimate meaning, look at the Big Dipper."

Facing south, he gazed at it and was filled with doubt. One night, he attained realization. He then went to seek out [Zhao]jing. Jing asked, "Who is it that has come? The Master said, "Neither a person nor a self.
Jing asked, "If you are neither a person nor a self, what exactly are you? The Master said, "When hungry, I eat; when tired, I sleep. Jing could not resolve this.
Just then, Tieshan had returned from Goryeo and was staying at Shishuang, so the Master went there.
Upon seeing him, Iron Mountain sensed that the Master had attained a point of enlightenment, so he asked, "Where is your hermitage? The Master replied, "Ruzhou.
Iron Mountain asked, "What is the countenance of the founding ancestor Fengxue like? The Master said, "Stop, Teacher;
it would take nearly twenty years of effort to explain it all at once. Iron Mountain then seized his throat and asked, "What is the meaning of the word 'Mu' (No)?"
The Master said, "I have recently come from Tanzhou and have not received news from Hubei. Sanshan said, "That is not it; say it again. The Master said, "When did you leave Goryeo, O Monk?
Sanshan said, "That is not it either; say it once more. The Master let out a shout, shook his sleeves, and departed.

Sanshan said, "This brother is well-versed in all things, yet he has one great ailment: he claims to have attained enlightenment. The Master was deeply moved and accepted [Sanshan’s] iron-like [admonition].

Shan revealed the subtle and great Dharma-gate. Later, he lived in seclusion at Guangzhou, practicing alone in both walking and sitting for seventeen years before finally attaining transcendent realization.
He proclaimed universally: "The Dharma has no fixed form; it accords with the conditions that meet it as its essence.

Wielding the Vajra-sword, swallowing the thorny *kṣīrikā* fruit, one cuts off the tongues of the monks and sits upon the very crown of Vairocana. One erects a single blade of grass and makes it ten feet long."
The six golden bodies: take the sixteen-foot golden body and treat it as a single blade of grass.
This is neither the drum-beat of Heyishan nor the separate transmission outside the teachings; it is simply to leave one with not even an inch of thread upon them.

When the moon is cold in the autumn sky and the cold ashes flare into flame—here, to call this "Buddhadharma" is to fall into hell like a shot arrow; to not call it "Buddhadharma" is likewise to fall into hell.
Like an arrow shot from a bow. O virtuous ones, how ultimately do you understand this? To open your mouth is to lose your body and forfeit your life;
not to open your mouth is to rot away your tongue. Have you not seen the Boatman say: "For twenty years at Yaoshan, where I hid my body there was no trace;
where there was no trace, I did not hide my body"? Although he proclaimed it thus, he opened the Buddha’s wisdom.
Behold! He sets up the great round mirror, erects the banner of nirvana, and raises high the Prajñā. Striking and singing are raised together;
he simultaneously carries both the provisional and the ultimate. Illumination and function occur at once. Yet when viewed through the true eye, all these are merely idle household accoutrements;
they have no connection whatsoever with the concerns of us monks. Holding up his whisk, he said: "Do you understand?"
Chan Master Bijing Baogin of Lingjiu on Mount Wutai in Daizhou was a dharma successor of Chan Master Zhen of Jinyun. He was a native of Yongshou in Qianzhou and his surname was Shi.
Both his parents were devoted to the good. At that time, a śramaṇa presented a statue of Avalokiteśvara to his mother and instructed her, saying, "Serve it with reverence."

He prayed, "May a son of wisdom be born. Before long, a master was indeed born. A brilliant white light shone resplendently, illuminating the room. At the age of six, he received the precepts from Dharma Master Yunji Wen and became a novice monk (*śrāmaṇera*).

Upon receiving the full monastic precepts (*upasampadā*), he traveled extensively to various lecture halls to exhaustively investigate the principles of *Dharmalakṣaṇa* (Characteristics of Phenomena) and *Faxiang* (Dharma Characteristics).
After some time, he said, "Is this sufficient to bring an end to birth and death? Thereupon, he abandoned them and departed. At that time, there was Ruhu... [text fragment].
Master Zhen was expounding the Dharma at Jin-yun. The Master went to visit him, and [Master Zhen] showed him the essentials of the Way. The Master gave rise to a great state of doubt.
Once, while carrying a basket and following Master Hai to gather vegetables in the garden, he suddenly became motionless and did not stir for three periods of time before finally awakening.

Master Hai asked, "Have you entered meditative absorption? The Master replied, "Absorption has nothing to do with movement or stillness. Master Hai asked, "Who is it that has nothing to do with movement or stillness?"

The Master raised the basket; Hai refused. The Master set the basket on the ground and stood with his hands folded; Hai still refused. The Master let out a shout. Hai stepped forward, struck at his chest, and said, "Speak quickly!
The Master struck Hai’s chest and knocked him down. Hai laughed and said, "My worldly toil has briefly ceased, yet my power of meditative concentration is not yet deep enough.
I must cause the path of the mind to be cut off and penetrate the Patriarchal Barrier; only then will I [attain] the Great..."
The Dharma can indeed be clarified. Later, he stayed at Mount Emei, subsisting daily on pine and cypress and not touching his mat for three years.
One day, hearing the sound of trees being felled, he attained great enlightenment. He went to see Mazu Daoyi (Hai). Mazu drew a circle on the ground;
the Master brushed it away with his sleeve. Mazu then drew another circle; the Master added a stroke within it and brushed that away as well.
Hǎi drew it again as before. The Master added another stroke to form a cross and then wiped it away. Hǎi drew it again as before.
The Master added four corners to the cross to form a swastika (卍) and then wiped it away.
Hǎi then drew thirty circular marks in total. The Master answered each one in detail. Hǎi said, "Only now do you understand the vast and supreme nature of the Buddha-dharma."
"It is so. You should go to the north; there your Way will flourish greatly.

Previously, while the Master was in meditative concentration, he had seen a mountain of great beauty, with multi-storied pavilions and magnificent halls shimmering in gold and green. Within it, various Buddhas and fifty-two Bodhisattvas were practicing the Path.
One of them beckoned the Master and said, "This is the Secret Demon Rock of Wutai. It was here that you cultivated the Way in a previous life."
"The sacred remains are still here; why have you forgotten them? Having awakened, he then traveled to Mount Wutai.
On the way, he encountered a woman with disheveled hair wearing five-colored robes and tattered garments, walking slowly barefoot with a black mastiff following behind her.
The Master asked, "Where are you going? She replied, "I am entering the mountains. The Master asked, "What will you do there? She replied, "I shall do nothing at all. After a long silence...

He then vanished; those traveling with him all failed to see him. Some said he was a transformation-body of Mañjuśrī. The Master then settled at the mountain and built the Lingjiu Hermitage to dwell in.
His reputation and brilliance were increasingly manifest, and news of him reached people from all directions, many traveling more than a thousand li to hear him.

Those who came to offer him provisions and grain arrived in daily abundance. In the fifth year of the Zhiheng era (1358), the Emperor Shundi dispatched an envoy with an imperial decree to the capital, where he was treated with great reverence.

He was ordered to reside at Haerin Temple, but he declined on the grounds of illness. The Emperor subsequently bestowed upon him the title "Jijiao Yuanming" (Tranquil Illumination and Perfect Clarity).

When Emperor Taizu, the August Founder, ascended the throne, he issued an edict for the Master to come to Nanjing. There, the Master had an audience with the Emperor in the inner palace, where the Emperor inquired about the general principles of the Buddha-dharma.
The Emperor established the Pujihui (Universal Salvation Assembly) at Mount Zhongshan and selected ten monks of high conduct to preside over its affairs;
the Master was among them. He received exceedingly generous imperial favors and was personally granted a twelve-line poem written by the Emperor’s own hand. Not long after,
He manifested a slight illness. His disciples requested that he leave behind his final words. The Master said, "Even the Dharma-treasure of the Tripitaka is but old paper;
what could my words possibly accomplish? He passed away with a serene expression. He was sixty-five years of age and fifty-nine years since his ordination.
Upon cremation, five-colored śarīras were obtained; his teeth, tongue, and prayer beads remained unburnt.
Chan Master Lizhong Cheng of Ciguang Temple in Hangzhou,
a descendant of the twenty-third generation under Nanyue and a dharma heir of Chan Master Lian of Jingci Temple, was born into the Sun family of Qiantang. He first visited Master Zufang Lian.

The Duke requested further instruction on the next couplet regarding the story of the mountain being burned by fire in the twelfth month. The Master offered this verse: "The white clouds obscure the old tracks;
In the twelfth month, the fire burning the mountain is bright red. Once again, the breeze of compassion comes to fan it, Turning the freezing cold into a warm glow.
The Duke held him in high esteem.

Chan Master Qianyan Yuanchang of Mount Fulong in Wuzhou was a dharma successor of Chan Master Zhongfeng Ben. He was the son of the Dong family of Xiaoshan in Yue; his family lineage had long honored Confucianism.
At the age of nine, he attended an external tutor, and all the books that came before his eyes were committed to memory. At nineteen, he received the tonsure at Wulin.
At Lingzhi Temple, the Chancellor Huixing was hosting a meal for the monastics. The Master joined the assembly to receive offerings.
Just then, Zhongfeng was seated among them and called out, "How do you spend your daily life? The Master replied, "I recite the Buddha's name. Zhongfeng asked, "Where is the Buddha now?

The Master hesitated, and Zhongfeng rebuked him with a stern voice. The Master then knelt and requested the essentials of the Dharma; Zhongfeng bestowed upon him the instruction of Zhaozhou’s "No-Phrase" (Wuhua).
"San! Thereupon, he bound himself with reeds in the midst of Mount Lingyin. Before long, he was moved again due to other affairs;
thus, following the conditions of the world, ten years passed in an instant. He returned once more to Lingyin and remained there for three years without his side ever touching the mat.

Later, while traveling to Wangting, he attained realization upon hearing the cry of a magpie. He hurried to see Master Feng to present the cause of his awakening, but Feng again rebuked him. The Master left in a fit of indignation.

He returned home. As night was falling into silence, he suddenly heard the sound of a rat eating cat-food and falling into its bowl. He attained a sudden, profound awakening. He went back to consult Feng. Feng asked, "Why did Zhaozhou say 'no'? The Master said, "A rat ate the cat-food. Feng said, "Not yet. The Master said, "The food-bowl has broken. Feng asked, "What is it like after it has broken? The Master said, "Only when it is ground into fine shards is it truly gone. Feng said, "After it is ground into shards, what then? The Master said, "It becomes a brick. Feng said, "After it becomes a brick, what then? The Master said, "It is used to build a wall. Feng said, "After it is used to build a wall, what then? The Master said, "It is plastered over with mud. Feng said, "After it is plastered with mud, what then? The Master said, "It is painted white. Feng said, "After it is painted white, what then? The Master said, "It is hung with a banner. Feng said, "After it is hung with a banner, what then? The Master said, "It is blown down by the wind. Feng said, "After it is blown down by the wind, what then? The Master said, "It is swept away by the current. Feng said, "After it is swept away by the current, what then? The Master said, "It is swallowed by a fish. Feng said, "After it is swallowed by a fish, what then? The Master said, "The fish is caught by a man. “When I was clearing the wilderness, I dug up a worn-out axe-head at the site of the Dharma Hall. It has been with me for a long time, brothers.
If there is anyone among you who can make use of it, I shall entrust it to you with both hands. But if you are unable to bear its weight, I shall keep it; why such a desperate hurry?”
"It would be better to cast it onto a heap of refuse, letting it be scorched by the sun and buffeted by the wind. Suddenly, he seized his staff, struck once, and said:
"Whipping up the iron ox to plow the great earth—who could plant crabapples at the bottom of a well?

In the spring of the twenty-sixth year of the Hongwu era, an imperial edict was issued summoning eminent monks of high conduct from throughout the realm. The Master was among those nominated to respond to the summons.
His Majesty approved. In the autumn, he received an imperial decree to perform a ritual at Mount Lu; when the ceremony was completed, he again received an edict bestowing upon him a set of robes.
That winter, he received an imperial decree to ascend and reside at Mount Jing. Entering the hall, he said:

"Since the birth of all Buddhas, those who have preached the Dharma like clouds and rain are beyond counting. Today, at Mount Jing, we shall temporarily borrow empty space for a mouth and Mount Sumeru for a tongue."

He proclaimed the Dharma-gate of the non-duality of the ultimate and the conventional. Sentient and insentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions simultaneously praised him with one voice:
"Excellent, excellent! Rare, rare indeed! Is there anyone among the assembly who does not secretly resent this?
Come forth and meet the staff! [The Master] took up the staff, struck once, and said: "Observe closely the Dharma King."

Dharma. Such is the Dharma of the Dharma King. [The Master] ascends the hall: "Someone has come from Mount Lu and brought a letter from Mount Huading, reporting that the white-fanged tiger of Nanshan is actually hiding its fangs and subduing its claws within the Dragon Abyss;

while the crimson-scaled carp of the Eastern Sea leaps directly to the peak of Vulture Mountain, surging through the waves. Good assembly, how could the entire Great Canon ever have spoken of such a thing?"
Although so it may be, the staff of Mount Lingjiu has not yet granted a pardon. [The Master] picks up his staff, draws a line, and says:
"The immortal Zhang Guolao does not care for medicinal gourds. He leans on the staff and descends from the seat.

Suddenly, on the twenty-third day of the tenth month, he said to the assembly: "Difficult, difficult! A beautiful young maiden of sixteen ascends a high mountain; even this old monk cannot support her."
Having finished speaking, he became silent.

Chan Master Jianxin Laifu of Lingyin Monastery in Hangzhou was a successor of Chan Master Yue of Jing Mountain. He was the son of the Wang family of Fengcheng in Nanchang and received the tonsure under [Master Yue].
In a monastery to the west of the town, he vowed to eliminate all external conditions and directly clarify the wondrous purport of *nirvāṇa*.
After a long time, his entire being became free from obstruction. He visited Nanchu, who approved of him; he remained there serving as the internal registrar (*naishi*).

He first resided at Dingshui in Yue, where he built a cottage by the eastern stream called "Reed Hermitage" (*Fuan*) to express his filial intent toward his parents in Muzhou. Closing the gate, he addressed the assembly: "My physical form is like withered wood."
A hundred thoughts turn to ash. Valley monkeys and wild cranes harbor bitter suspicions. The thatched gate stands alone shut amidst the rain upon the green pines;
even when meeting people, my smiling mouth is too weary to open. He once composed a verse on the White Ox: "Plowing the clouds, he never stops east of the Sea Gate;

He gathers and releases at the small peaks of Mount Laṅkā. On the open ground, he has already forgotten the power of taming; Who in the Snowy Mountains knows his tracks of coming and going? [He] released him back to roam free.

At Jeta’s Grove, he followed the sheep and deer; planting the seeds of the *dharma*-flower, he became a companion to the elephants and dragons. Though they share the same hue within the celestial railing, their horns and heads differ;
in the crystal pond, there bloom jade lotuses. In the winter of the first year of Hongwu, he was summoned for his lofty conduct to preach the Dharma at Mount Zhong.
He was granted meals within the inner court. The Master had a reputation for his literary talent; the Emperor commanded his attendants to retrieve and examine his writings, praising them incessantly.
At that time, Prince Chu of Shu was the object of Grand Emperor Taizu’s particular affection.

He ordered the Confucian scholars Li Shijing, Su Boheing, and others to engage the Master in discussions on the Way every day without fail. Prince Chu treated the Master with great reverence and commissioned him to compose the *Zuoxin* (Seated Mind).
He composed four admonitions—*Guandao*, *Chongben*, *Jingxian*, and *Sizhen*—which were posted in his palace for his own edification.
In the twenty-fourth year, when the Hu faction was apprehended in Shanxi, Master Ju and others who had frequented the Hu residence were charged with the crime and executed.
Chan Master Wuzhi Ke of Jingci Monastery in Hangzhou was a successor of Chan Master Ming of Lingyin. He was the son of the Li family of Linhai in Taizhou.

At the age of twelve, he entered Shimen Temple as a "crow-chaser" (a novice). At nineteen, he received full ordination and became a *bhikṣu*. Thereafter, he sighed, saying: "What is truly precious..."

For one who is a bhikṣu, the primary task is to seek a thorough understanding of the essence of the mind. If one remains entangled within the appearances of words and letters, when will one ever be able to attain liberation?
Consequently, he took up his staff and traveled throughout all directions, yet for a long time he found no conditions that accorded with his realization.

Eventually, he visited Master Pujue Ming at Lingyin Monastery. During a brief exchange of questions and answers, his doubts were suddenly dispelled. Master Pujue approved of him and appointed him to serve as the Hall Superintendent.
The Administrator (Sī) returned to Shimen. Master Zhen of Bairyam invited him to occupy the position of *upādhyāya*.

In the sixth year of the Zhizhi era, he entered the world at Daixiong Monastery in Tiantai, then moved to Long'en, and subsequently filled the seat at Bairyam. The following year, he moved to Longhua. He occupied that seat for fifteen autumns, restoring all that had fallen into ruin.
Thereupon, he built the Xiuan-an hermitage in the western valley and daily cultivated the practice of the Pure Land, saying, "This is itself Chan."

It was his merit. How could one forcibly clarify the similarities and differences? In the sixth year of the Hongwu era, the Master was summoned to occupy the seat at Zhongzhu Temple in Hangzhou by order of the Prefectural Marquis.

The Master reluctantly accepted. Upon reaching the riverbank, the veteran monks of Jingci Temple led their assembly to intercept him on the road and escorted him into the temple to take the position. The Master declined, but they would not let him; his expression became dejected.

Yi resided there for two years. He retired after striking the drum with his hand and returned to lie down in the bamboo courtyard. Suddenly, he manifested illness; sitting upright facing west, he said to those around him, "I am about to pass away.
When the assembly requested a verse, the Master replied, "In our school, there is fundamentally no speech.

He then joined his palms and recited the Buddha’s name until the sound gradually faded and he entered nirvana. During the cremation, his teeth remained intact, threaded like beads. His remains were enshrined.
Those with beneficial colors, such as gold, silver, and crystal, fill the earth and are hidden within dragon stupas.
Master Wuya Feihuan of Linggu Monastery in Nanjing was a dharma successor of Chan Master Wushi Yuchan; he was a native of Xi'an in Quzhou and followed Jiefeng as his teacher.

Master Sengfeng asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "Empty space has neither front nor back. Sengfeng pointed to the temple bell and instructed him to compose a verse. The Master said:
"Rolled forth from the furnace of a hundred refinements, Empty space originally never gathers dust.

Now it hangs upon the heads of men; When struck, its great sound pervades the nine realms. At that time he was twelve years old. Sengfeng esteemed his talent and immediately had him take the monastic precepts.
Fahai. In the Dinghai year of the Yongle era, Emperor Taizong Wenhuang held a memorial service at Changling. He summoned the Master to appear before him;

his responses were to the Emperor's satisfaction, and the Emperor greatly rewarded and bestowed gifts upon him. He was then ordered to reside at Linggu Monastery. In the spring of the Gengzi year, the Emperor established a Dharma assembly.
When the Master appeared to take no notice of it, his disciples questioned him about it. The Master smiled and said, "I have a matter of my own that is most urgent. What [business is there in this]?"
When he was about to pass away, he wrote a verse, saying: "Life and death drift on, severed from worldly ties; By your grace, I enjoy eternal peace for all time.
This time, casting off my hands, I return to emptiness; The snow has cleared, the clouds have vanished, and the moon is full. Thereupon, he passed away.
Master Taichu Qiyuan of Sanfeng Temple in Luoyang was a native of Japan. At the age of nineteen, he traveled to the Great Kingdom (China) and studied under forty-five spiritual mentors (*kishi*).
Finally, he received the Dharma from Master Jiefeng. Later, he resided at Sanfeng. One day, he wrote a verse, saying:
"Living, it is an iron mask; Dying, it is an iron mask. With a single blow, it shatters into a hundred pieces— The bright sun circles around."
Tiéwéi (Cakravāḍa). He cast aside his writing brush and passed away.
His stupa was erected to the south of the monastery.
*Jìdēnglù*, Scroll Five; *Jìdēnglù*, Scroll Six.
Compiled by the Drum Mountain lineage-holding śramaṇa Yuánxián,
of the twenty-fourth generation below Nanyuè in the Linjì school.
Chan Master Wanfeng Shiwei of Mount Dengwei in Suzhou was a successor of Chan Master Fulong Chang. He was the son of the Jin family in Leqing, Wenzhou.

At the age of thirteen, he left home to become a monk under the lecturer Sheng of Yanqing in his native county; at sixteen, he shaved his head; and at nineteen, he changed his robes to study [the Way].
Chan. Having heard of the reputation of Master Zhiyan of Hupao in Hangzhou, he went there to pay his respects. Zhiyan gave him the kōan of the "Three Not-Sos.
He then returned to Mingzhou and established a hermitage at the ruins of Fotuo Temple on Mount Dapeng to cultivate the Way.
One day, while I was in a state of profound doubt and distress, I suddenly heard Master Zong of the monastery citing Baizhang’s question to Guishan:
"It cannot be called a 'pure vase'; what should it be called? Guishan kicked over the pure vase and walked away.
Unconsciously, my mass of doubt was shattered, and I spoke this verse: "Toppling and tumbling, old Nanquan, Has caused my diligent practice to be cut short by half."
If one can personally realize this right now, how could one not advance and strike a fist to the chest? Thereupon, he went to Huading Peak to visit Wu Jian to seek a definitive resolution.
Wu Jian asked, "The myriad dharmas all return to the One; to what does the One return? The Master stepped forward, paid his respects, and said, "I hope you are well.
Wu Jian asked again, "What is the Way? The Master replied, "The Way is that which cannot be spoken of. Wu Jian said, "Not..."

"Regarding the Way, what more is there to say? The Master said, "I specifically want the Master to have doubts. Yuanjian said, "To have doubts is an error. The Master said, "Not to have doubts is also an error.
Yuanjian gave a shout; the Master also gave a shout. Yuanjian shouted again; the Master also shouted. He then shook his sleeves and departed.
He returned to Mount Dapeng and lived there for ten years. Later, he went to Fulong to see Qianyan. Qianyan then—
The question was asked: "That which is not mind, not Buddha, and not a thing—what is it? The Master struck a circular mark with his sitting cloth (*zuoju*) and stood with his hands crossed.
Yanguan retired. The next day he saw him again. Yanguan asked, "With what do you come to meet this old monk?
The Master held up his fist and said, "I meet the Master here. Yanguan said, "Dead!"
"Once it has been burned away, where will you establish yourself and find your livelihood? The Master replied, "The bubble arises and the bubble perishes, yet the water remains;
the wind ceases and the waves subside, and the moon reflects in the pool. Yunyan asked again, "Do you not wish to seek further instruction and receive the precepts?

The Master covered his ears and departed. On the following day, Yunyan ordered the Master to enter the hall and lead the assembly. One day, while ascending the hall, Yunyan cited the verse on the lotus leaf in a windless breeze.
"When there is movement, there must be fish swimming. The Master stepped forward from the assembly, gave a shout, and stroked his sleeves as he departed.
Yunyan (Yan Yin) spoke in verse: "Deep green chrysanthemums fill the eyes; autumn is here. Baizhang sits upright atop the azure peak.

Lightly bringing forth the phrase 'no guest, no host,' A single shout makes the waters of a thousand rivers flow backward. Upon seeing this verse, the Master resigned from his post and subsequently went to Mount Song at Lanxi.

He lived in a thatched hut on a mountain. Later, when Yuanran invited him with a letter, he did not come; instead, Yuanran sent someone to deliver a Dharma robe and a portrait of his head (top-phase) to him.
Only then did the Master begin to propagate the Dharma. At the end of the Yuan dynasty, he moved his staff to Dengweishan in Suzhou, where he founded a monastery.
His name was Sheng'en. The influence of his Way spread far and wide, and those among both monastics and laity who turned toward him increased in number.
On the nineteenth day of the first month in the fourteenth year of the Hongwu era, having gathered the assembly and finished his final instructions, he sat cross-legged and spoke this verse:
"Seventy-nine years of a single flavor, weeding the field; letting go at the precipice, the bright sun shines in the sky. Having finished speaking, he passed away. His secular age was seventy-nine.

He had sixty years of seniority as a monk (*saṃgha-vatsara*). His *kaṅkha* (relic chamber) remained for thirteen days, his countenance appearing as if alive. On the thirteenth day of the second month, his entire body was enshrined in a stupa to the west of the monastery.
Chan Master Wuyong Shougui of Tiantong in Hangzhou was the son of the Zhen family of Pujiang in Wuzhou. He entered the [monastery of] Kanghou...

Shan was the head of the monastic community. Upon visiting Qianyan, he felt as though he had attained a profound realization. Subsequently, he met with the various elders at Zhongfeng, who said to him, "Though the thousand rivers differ, the bright moon remains one;
from this day forward, I have no further doubts. In the year Gengyin of the Zhizheng era, he took charge of Tianlong Monastery.
Within a few years, all its major and minor facilities were complete, and it became a truly magnificent monastery. Later, on the day he manifested his passing, he wrote:
The verse says: A single snail in a stinking shell, filthy within and without; with a flick of the hand he departs, ringing his bell through the void.
With a single finger from the devas and nāgas, it is as if today were yesterday. He cast down his brush and passed away.
Chan Master Weian Deran of Songyin in Songjiang Prefecture was the son of the Zhang family of that district. In his youth, he shaved his head under Master Guyong Wuyong;
subsequently, he visited Qianyan, and upon hearing his formal teachings (*tichang*), he attained sudden and thorough enlightenment. Later, he succeeded him as the abbot of that seat.
Entering the hall for a discourse, he said: "The new year begins, and all things are renewed. He then suddenly took up his staff and said: "This staff, yesterday..."
Last night it drew forth its shoots; this morning it has shed its buds. The flower opens its five petals, and its fragrance fills the great trichiliocosm.
Tell me, does this suffice for the Buddha-dharma at the head of the New Year? (He plants his staff and lets out a shout. Entering the hall: Heaven has no gate; earth has no door.
A swift and capable monk may come and go as he pleases. The *maṇi* jewel within the treasury illuminates the ten directions;
the peach blossoms in the cave compete to bloom in a thousand petals. Borrowing the spring breeze from beyond kalpas, they respond to the pitch-pipes of the present age.

At midnight, the sea deity gazes upon the shark’s pearl; its light is suspended upon the tree of Mount Fusang. (He lets out a shout. Entering the hall: "The wax figure serves as the test. Only then...
Today, at the conclusion of the ninety-day retreat, the merits are being evaluated and the ultimate truth discerned.

The Yellow-Faced Old Gautama has tied up the mouth of his sack, causing hundreds of thousands of devas and humans to all suffer defeat. At Songyin, however, the retreat is not conducted in such a manner.

Making a gesture with his hands as if rowing a boat, he said: "I, this mountain monk, am now launching an iron boat without a bottom; I invite the entire assembly to enter the Great [Dharma] together."
"Round Enlightenment Ocean has gone off to play! He gave a shout and said, "Look at this fixed compass.
Chan Master Konggu Jǐnglóng of Kaiyuán Monastery in Hangzhou, a successor of Chan Master Báilián Ān, was the son of the Chén family of Dōngtíng in Sū. As a child...
At that time, he abstained from meat and sat in the lotus posture as if in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

He once sought instruction on the essentials of the Way from Lanyun of Mount Bian and visited all the great masters of the lakes and seas without exception. Later, he took Shi’an of Tiger Hill as his teacher.

In the second year of the Xuande era, he received the full precepts at Zhaoling Monastery in Hangzhou. Thereupon, he followed Shi’an and resided at Lingyin for seven years, after which he went to Mount Tianmu to pay his respects.
He stayed at Zu’s stupa for one year, where he practiced with intense diligence and underwent a sudden realization. He then went to Lan Yun to disclose his insight, and Yun certified his attainment.
Initially, he resided at Zhengchuan Monastery on West Lake; in his later years, he moved to Kaiyuan.
He passed away and was interred at Xuji Mountain on West Lake. His collected works, the *Konggu ji*, are extant in the world.
Chan Master Wunian Shengxue of Jiufeng,
Wujiang Prefecture, successor to Chan Master Deng Weiwei of the twenty-fifth generation under Nanyue, was a native of Yingzhou, Suizhou, Dede County. His surname was Chen.
At the age of nine, he took the tonsure under Master Yuan of Baolin Temple in his native commandery. Realizing that his own spiritual matter remained unclear, he went to consult Master Wumen.

Wumen showed him the koan, "The myriad dharmas return to one. Later, he entered Mount Song to dwell in seclusion. One day, he attained realization, composing this verse: "For years at East Mountain, the mist hung thick;
I leaned on the railing all day, waiting for the clear sky. Last night, suddenly the frosty heavens rose with the moon."
The myriad phenomena are fully manifested within a single mirror. Thereupon, he visited Mount Dengwei to consult Wanfeng; Wanfeng verified this for him with a verse.
He then returned to Baolin, where his reputation for the Way became widely renowned. King Zhao of Chu built a monastery to invite the Master to reside there.
The Master asked the assembly, "What is the one phrase of Bodhidharma’s direct pointing? The assembly was speechless. The Master spoke on their behalf: "Before the Five Milk Peaks."
Regarding his discourse at Shaoshi: During the Hongwu era, the Emperor Taizu summoned him to the Fengtian Hall and personally inquired about the essentials of the Dharma.

The Master presented a verse, which greatly pleased the Emperor; the Emperor then composed poetry and prose to bestow upon him as gifts. On the twenty-ninth day of the third month of the third year of the Yongle era (the year of Yiyou), he spoke a verse, saying:
"The World-Honored One was seventy-nine; at eighty, he reached the limit of non-thought. He shattered the Flower Treasury."
The sea remains as ever, its waters joining the sky. He passed away with solemn dignity. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa at Shiziyuan.
He was posthumously titled Chan Master Qingfu Guanghui. He was a dharma successor of Chan Master Cizhou Ji.
Chan Master Shouchang Xizhu Benlai was a native of Chongren in Fuzhou. His surname was Pei. At the age of seven, he left home to become a monk at Guanyin Temple in his hometown.
At thirteen, he visited Yifeng Ning, who transmitted to him the methods of Chan meditation.
Diligently investigating the matter within his own person, one day he suddenly realized that his body was like empty space and his mind was devoid of boundaries or limits.
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, he did not know who it was. Suddenly, hearing someone reciting the *Sūtra of Purity*, which says:
"Internally observing the mind, the mind has no mind," he attained a sudden awakening. He composed a verse, saying: "For many years I wandered abroad, losing my true soul; today..."
Their meeting was quite extraordinary. Beside him stood a golden-haired stone lion; turning its head, it swallowed the Iron Kunlun.
Thereupon, [Dongshan] went to see Yifeng Ning to present what he had realized. Ning did not grant his approval. He then went to Jiangdong in Guixi to erect a hermitage and dwell there.
After seven years, he finally attained enlightenment. By that time, Ning had already passed away. He then went to Jinshan to see Cizhou.

Ji received the seal of approval (*kṣānti*) and retired to Seongsu Temple on Geumgangsan Mountain. Later, when Prince Ning heard that the Master’s realization had surpassed all others, he dispatched envoys three times to invite him, yet the Master ultimately did not go.
The Prince further presented a verse to inquire about the Way, to which the Master replied with the essentials of spiritual cultivation.
The Prince was greatly delighted and bestowed upon the Master the title of "Great Chan Master Hwigwang Pujō Dongo Wontong of the Western River and Western India."
His reputation spread far and wide from this point on, and students came from all quarters in great numbers. He subsequently moved to Shouchang in Xincheng, where he established a great monastery.
Entering the hall, he said: "The flowers are brilliant; the sun's orb is crimson. The Dharma of the mind shines forth, penetrating everywhere.
The nostrils of the patch-robed monk are vast beneath his great head; a surging breath fills the universe. With eyes emptying the four seas, he has no worldly concerns—only..."
This staff-bearer holds the staff in his hand; if he wishes to go west, he goes west; if he wishes to go east, he goes east.

*Zhuo!* (A knock) He descends from the seat. Small Assembly Sermon: "Clear! Clear! Clear! A single expanse of long sky, its light shining bright and pure. Rest! Rest! Rest! Clouds fly high on their own, and waters flow of their own accord.
With eyes opened wide and the whole body permeated, there is no front or back; throughout the ten directions and all dust-motes of worlds, one may roam at will. — Recorded by Futián of Shànguān.

The temple had fallen into ruin, and he requested the Master to restore it. When the work was nearly finished, one day he sat cross-legged in meditation after burning incense and asked for a brush to write this verse:
"This old beggar—when will his teaching ever end? Tumbling and turning, he lets himself drift with the current; Whether he is a sage or an ordinary person, people do not understand.
Hah! Come, come, come! Go, go, go! The sea is deep and still, the sky is clear and pure; The wind is fresh and the moon is bright. He then cast [the brush] away.
He passed away while holding his writing brush. His secular age was sixty-eight and his monastic seniority was fifty-five. His disciples enshrined his true body in the Shibaotang Hall.
He was a Dharma successor of Chan Master Fancharu Jun.
Chan Master Wuji of Donglin in Puzhou was a native of Shu. At the age of twenty, he emerged from worldly entanglements and constructed a hermitage by binding bamboo together.
He applied himself with unremitting diligence; he would not even look at a written note the size of four fingers, practicing only through "blindly striking" and blunt effort.
Later, he attained great penetration and great enlightenment, composing a verse that says: "Quiescent illumination has no above or below; its radiance penetrates everywhere. Originally..."

Chan Master Taichu of Mount Tiantong, whose courtesy name was Ziyu, was a native of Wenling. His family had been Confucian scholars for generations; the Master himself was a man of noble character and remarkable talent.
Dazhi’s poetry and prose were all extraordinary; many scholars and officials held him in high esteem.

One day, he abandoned his former life and entered Zunseng Temple to "select for Buddhahood" (seek enlightenment), disciplining himself according to the Vinaya and completely casting off his habits of aristocratic extravagance. He traveled beyond the ridges to visit various teachers, gaining a great reputation within the monastic communities.
After a long time, he ceased his travels and returned to Min. It happened that the seat at Ba’en Temple in Nanjian was vacant, and the local administration...
Shou Chenmi heard of the Master’s reputation and appointed him to lead the community. Not long after, Zhen Dexiu came from Daguai to invite him;
he resided there for twenty years, and the assembly grew to a thousand members. The Master’s exposition of the Dharma was versatile, profound, and vast, not yielding to the great patriarchs of old.

Once Dexiu had retired from office, he frequently visited the Master, and as they conversed at ease on the Way, there was none who did not become spiritually intoxicated. Generally speaking, the Master—
He received people with sincerity and simplicity. Initially, he established a gateway by demonstrating the great harmony between Confucianism and Buddhism, enabling them to enter;
ultimately, he revealed the ultimate pinnacle of his own Dharma as the inner chamber, providing them with a place of true refuge. Therefore, the refined scholars held him in high esteem.
Chan Master Zhongguan Zhao, Haeyun Jin’am, was his preceptor. He once instructed Haeyun, saying:
"What you desire is merely words and language; henceforth, cease all of them. Let your body and mind become like withered wood or extinguished ashes.
When the present time is exhausted and your practice reaches full maturity, undergo a 'great death' and let no residual breath remain. When that moment arrives..."
"Only when you can suddenly awaken to self-reflection may you truly meet me. Later, he was captured by the Yuan army along with Haiyun and crossed northward to Shuofang.
The Emperor of the Yuan dynasty conferred upon him the title of Master Ciyun Zhengjue. When the Master was about to pass away, the immortal Yang Zhishen requested a verse.
The Master took up his brush and wrote the verse on his behalf: Seven... (Note: The text provided ends mid-verse; the translation reflects the available portion.)
Thirteen years have passed like a flash of lightning. As I depart, I shall open a single thread for you:
the mud ox flies across the sea from the east; neither in heaven nor among men can he be found. A guest asked, "When will the Master depart? The Master replied, "Three days hence.
It was the twenty-seventh day of the fifth month. On the first day of the sixth month, he indeed passed away without illness.
Chan Master Wuyi of Xuefeng Qiyin was a native of Huai’an. His surname was Nie. Having become a monk, he refused to confine himself to a single location and repeatedly visited renowned masters.

Later, he received the Dharma from Chan Master Fohai of Xuefeng. In the tenth year of the Dade era, the regional commander recommended him to take up residence at Xuefeng, where he remained for seven years.
He subsequently retired to the Western Hermitage. In the third year of the Huangqing era, he was again invited [to serve].

By imperial decree, he was appointed to reside there again and bestowed with the title "Buddha-Wisdom" (Fozhi). After six years, he retired from his duties. In the second year of the Taiding era, he was once more appointed to the foremost seat by imperial command.
He occupied this position for seven years; having resided at Xuefeng three times, he restored all that had fallen into ruin, creating a magnificent achievement for the Dharma gate.

I once wrote a preface to the Record of Xuefeng, in which I said: After Old Zhijue’s "single blow from Deshan" caused the bottom of the bucket to fall out, he attained a state where the moon was cold over the market stalls and the snow had cleared from Elephant Peak.
He took the essence of the *tīrtha* (clarified butter) in a single ladle and manifested great function through three balls.
It may be compared to the thundering of ten billion peals of lightning beneath the four heavens; for hundreds of generations, its resonance has only grown more vast.
Hong! All that you have bestowed as instruction flows forth from your breast, encompassing heaven and earth. It is like a single performance of the "Guangling" melody;
beneath it, the minor strings feel ashamed and can no longer produce a sound. He passed away in the second year of the Yuantong era and was interred in a stupa beside the Fohai Stupa.
The Great Chan Master Yuantong of Tongxuan Hermitage on Yuxi once composed one hundred questions to inspire his disciples.
Later, Wansong answered them and Linquan provided verses for each; both sets match the original number in one hundred. These works are now widely circulated throughout the world.
Chan Master Wujin Zudeng of Yunfeng on Mount Tiantai was the son of the Wang family of Siming.
He studied under Master Rixi Yong at Tianning Temple and asked, "The matter of birth and death is great, and impermanence is swift. I beg you for some instruction. Rixi said:

"Throughout the twelve periods of the day and night, investigate this closely and intimately. When you suddenly strike upon it, come back and ask again. The Master raised his voice and said, "Impermanence is swift;

the matter of birth and death is great. Before he had finished speaking, Xī gave a shout. The Master immediately prostrated himself. Xī asked, "What principle have you seen that you prostrate yourself like this?
The Master replied, "To open one's mouth is already an error. Xī nodded in approval, and the Master departed to travel and study elsewhere.
The various senior elders of the mountain followed him as he planted his staff atop Yunfeng Peak. For fifty springs and autumns, his shadow never left the mountain.

On the eighth day of the second month in the second year of the Hongwu era, he manifested a slight illness. When the night was nearly half over, he looked toward his attendants and asked, "Is the sky beginning to brighten?
They replied, "Not yet. Someone asked, "What will the Master do at this very moment? The Master broke into a smile and said, "In the past..."
An ancient worthy was sitting in illness when a monk asked, "Is there anyone who is not ill? The Worthy said, "There is. The monk asked, "What is this one who is not ill?
The Worthy said, "A-ya, A-ya. The Master [Zhaozhou] remained silent for a long while and then said, "Can such a thing as this be called being ill?
The assembly was speechless. The Master said, "The physical body is impermanent; seek realization early. The time has come; I am about to depart. His attendant...
He took up paper and asked for a verse. The Master said, "If I ultimately have no verse, would you not yet be permitted to die? The attendant pressed him even more insistently. Thereupon, he wrote:
"Birth and death, coming and going, Are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha. Overturning the five Sumerus, All is vast and open, without front or back.
Having set down his brush, he sat upright and passed away.
Chan Master Jing’an Zhuang of Mount Jingshan was a native of Taizhou. From childhood, he loathed the impurities of meat and held the secular world in low esteem.

His parents allowed him to leave home at Guangci Hermitage. After some time, he traveled extensively to study under various masters outside the conventional fold, thoroughly penetrating the source of the Zen lineage.

He once presided over two monasteries in the region of Yue; whenever things did not meet his expectations, he would immediately resign and depart. He subsequently went to rely upon Quanshi at Tianjie Monastery, where Quanshi placed him in charge.
He served as abbot twice. Not long after, he was appointed to Mount Jing. His spiritual influence flourished greatly.
In the twelfth year of the Yongle era, he entered the capital by imperial decree to assist in the compilation of the Great Canon. He resided at Tien-chieh Monastery for three years.

Although the Grand Preceptor Yao Gong and others submitted joint memorials recommending him to serve as the abbot, he firmly declined and did not accept. He returned to Mount Jing, where he passed away; his stupa was erected at Xiaochi on Shuiling.
The Chan Master Wukong of Shaolin (Shao-lin Pien-t'un) was the son of the Chen family of Xizhou in Kaifeng. He suddenly took leave of his parents to seek ordination.
His father said, "This child habitually extends his tongue past his nose; he possesses the marks of one who is no ordinary man. He was thus sent to Shaolin.
One day, he knelt before the Master and requested a Dharma name. The Master said, "The Way is fundamentally formless; how can there be a name?"
Regarding the existence of names, the Master said, "The Buddhas of the three periods of time all have name-titles. He then bestowed the Heart Sūtra upon him.
Upon reciting it until he realized that the five aggregates are entirely empty, he attained a sudden and great awakening. He then said, "If even this body is an illusion, where can one seek a name?
One day, his master wove a large basket with his own hands before him and said, "This flat basket is your name. The Master replied:
Since he was named Bian Dun (Flat Cask), there was no space within him. His teacher said, "Only through the 'Separate Transmission Outside the Teachings' can one truly accord with this principle.
Later, he went to the place where Master Shenchuan resided; for three days they engaged in debate, and his eloquence flowed like a rushing river.

Shenchuan remarked, "He is truly a lion of Shaolin; in the future, he will cut off the flow of all other currents. Subsequently, he traveled to Mount Emei, where he built a thatched hut to dwell in. One day...
Upon reaching the middle of the Yangtze River at Kuizhou, he said, "The Way is vast and boundless; it does not end with meeting people.
He then sat upright on the riverbank and passed away. *Jìdēnglù*, Scroll Six (End).
